title: Kent bowler Mahmud recalled by Bangladesh
description: Promotion-chasing Kent lose bowler Hasan Mahmud for the final two games of the County Championship season after he is recalled by Bangladesh.
fullText:
County Championship Division Two promotion chasers Kent have lost the services of bowler Hasan Mahmud for the final two matches of the season after he was recalled by Bangladesh.

The 26-year-old fast-medium has taken 30 wickets in seven matches in both the Championship and T20 Blast.

But he will now return to Bangladesh to prepare for their upcoming series with Afghanistan, West Indies and South Africa.

"We're disappointed to have lost Hasan's services for the County Championship run-in, but we respect the decision made by the BCB (Bangladesh Cricket Board) after constructive talks, and wish him well this winter," Simon Cook, Kent's director of cricket, told the club's website.

"While he will be a big miss, both of our other overseas bowlers, Keith Dudgeon and Khaled Ahmed, remain available for these last two matches of the summer."

Kent are third in the table, two points behind second-placed Northamptonshire but with two home games against the bottom two sides, Lancashire and Gloucestershire, to come.

title: Notre Dame still a top-5 team in ESPN’s Football Power Index
description: Notre Dame is off to a 2-0 start and No. 3 in the AP and Coaches polls. ESPN agrees that the Irish are a top-five team with recent CFP projections.
fullText:
After two weeks, Notre Dame football looks like a team on a mission, one that starts with a berth in the College Football Playoff.

With the Fighting Irish No. 3 in the latest US LBM Coaches Poll, they're off to a solid start following victories over Wisconsin and Rice. ESPN has made updates to its Football Power Index, PFI, and it's reflecting that Notre Dame is in fact a top-five team. Right now, ESPN's analytics have them as the No. 3 team in the country, behind No. 1 Ohio State and Texas, who beat the Buckeyes this past weekend.

The top-5 remain unchanged from last week, but aside from the Irish, in different order. It's safe to say that these are the best handful of teams in the country.

Notre Dame will host Michigan State in South Bend on Saturday evening. The last time the Irish and the Spartans squared off was on Sept. 23, 2017, a game Notre Dame won 38-18 in East Lansing.

title: Police officer assaulted during Old Firm cup match
description: The force said a 28-year-old man was arrested in connection with the incident during the Premier Sports Cup game.
fullText:
A Police Scotland officer was assaulted during Sunday's Old Firm match at Ibrox.

The force said a 28-year-old man was arrested in connection with the incident at the Premier Sports Cup game, which Rangers won 3-0.

Officers made a total of four arrests during the quarter-final clash, including a 55-year-old man for sectarian abuse.

A spokesperson said a 25-year-old man was arrested in connection with breach of the peace, while a fourth, aged 27, was arrested in connection with threatening and abusive behaviour and resisting arrest.

McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Chief Supt Stevie Dolan said the match, which kicked off at 12:00, passed without major incident and thanked the "majority of fans" for their conduct throughout the day.

He added: "A small number of offences were detected during the course of the event.

"These included one instance of police assault and a separate incident involving sectarian abuse.

"Behaviour such as this is never acceptable and will not be tolerated."

He added the 28-year-old and 55-year-old suspects would be reported to the procurator fiscal.

There were no away supporters at the game following a "temporary arrangement" which was reached after talks between the Glasgow clubs and the Scottish Professional Football League (SPFL).

It followed the Scottish FA's independent review into events surrounding last Season's Scottish Cup quarter-final at Ibrox, which was marred by unrest and pitch incursions from both sets of fans.

Derek McInnes' team will now face Aberdeen in the semi-finals while Hearts will play Hibs for a place in the final at Hampden on 13 December.

title: Davey reignites international ambitions with Wales
description: Uncapped Wales scrum-half Megan Davey's admits she almost called it quits before her recent call-up at the age of 26.
fullText:
Megan Davey's international ambitions have been reignited at her self-proclaimed 'old' age of 26.

Loughborough Lightning's record appearance holder considered going into full-time teaching when she did not make Wales' 2026 Six Nations squad.

Her hopes were dashed again when omitted from Sean Lynn's extended training squad for the WXV Global Series.

"There was a little bit of a wobble," admitted uncapped Davey.

"It's hard to keep going when you're at my age, you feel old in the game."

But the half-back received a call-up last month and is now part of the 39-strong squad which will take on South Africa, USA and Japan.

"There's always been something inside me, I know I can do it, it's the voice inside my head that's kept me going," she said.

"I was really happy that I got an opportunity."

Rose out of Wales WXV squad with injury

Davey qualifies for Wales through her grandfather from Llanelli but went through the English pathway system as a youngster.

"The avenue for under-20s was always really with England because it wasn't as set up with Wales, but now it's really good," she said.

"I'm a little bit older... now I feel like I can really do people proud."

And despite being a latecomer in camp, Davey says everyone has been welcoming.

"There's always that thing when you walk into an environment that's already established, you're like 'how am I going to do?' but I was really raring to go," she added.

"Obviously a bit sad that I wasn't in the squad to begin with, but you just crack on with what you're doing."

Live on BBC One, iPlayer and the BBC Sport website and app, with live text coverage

Davey has primarily trained at scrum-half with Wales and faces competition from Keira Bevan and Seren Lockwood.

And contrary to the stereotype of the position, the nines get along with no animosity.

"We all really enjoy each other's company. We want each other to do well, so there's never that hatred towards each other," said Davey, who has previously started at fly-half for Loughborough.

"Whoever goes out there and does the job first is the best pick for the team and you just need to back that completely."

Wales open their WXV campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on Friday, 18 September (19:15 BST), and any potential involvement would mean the world to Davey.

"Playing international rugby is such a privilege and I want to make everyone proud - my family, but also the coaches that have been behind me for the last 15 years of my journey," she said.

"It's just that final step, like 'I made it'. I'm really excited and hopefully it comes at some point."

title: How is NI squad shaping up for quadruple-header?
description: Northern Ireland will face four Nations League games in 11 days later this month with injuries, summer switches and individual form all making for an interesting selection when Michael O'Neill names his panel on Tuesday.
fullText:
Before changes to the international calendar brought in for this season, Northern Ireland would previously have already played their first two fixtures by this stage of September.

Under the new fixture list, manager Michael O'Neill will name a squad on Tuesday for a four-game window, beginning with an away trip to Georgia on 25 September and concluding at home to the same opposition on 5 October. In between they face Hungary in Belfast and Ukraine in Slovakia.

While not quite unprecedented - NI faced four Nations League games in 11 days during the summer of 2022 - the condensed schedule will certainly be a challenge for Northern Ireland and other countries with smaller population bases.

Unfortunately for O'Neill, injuries have already disrupted his plans too.

Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams

O'Neill 'hopeful' training centre plans progress

Star player Conor Bradley has not featured for club or country since knee surgery in January and O'Neill told BBC Sport NI this month that he always suspected the injury "was going to take longer than maybe some people were thinking" before adding it would be a "bonus" to see him in a green jersey before March 2027.

The 23-year-old has missed six of Northern Ireland's past 14 games through injury, and another thanks to a one-game suspension, but in many ways it has been a case of trying to replace the irreplaceable.

The Liverpool full-back tends to play in a more advanced role for his national side on the right-side of a 3-5-2 and, while O'Neill has other natural options for down the flank, none possess the same mix of attacking drive and defensive instinct.

Nor is Bradley the only injury concern before the squad announcement.

Midfielder Ali McCann injured his hamstring in Preston's 4-0 Carabao Cup defeat by Everton last month with his now former club manager Paul Heckingbottom saying his captain would be out for "months".

O'Neill has previously spoken about how the 26-year-old is the sort of player whose importance is highlighted in his absence and his injury leaves a hole in the starting XI alongside Fulham's Shea Charles in the preferred double-pivot.

The summer transfer window has again been a busy one for O'Neill's squad with a number of players making moves either on a permanent or loan basis.

Justin Devenny's Stoke career got off to a flying start with a double on his first start since his switch from Crystal Palace. A natural left-footer, he has given NI balance as a wing-back since his debut in June 2025.

A versatile player, Devenny has been turning out as a central midfielder for the Potters and could be one to fill the void left by McCann, as he did in the World Cup play-off defeat by Italy in March.

Oxford United's Brodie Spencer, if he is not needed to replace Bradley on the right, would then be an option to step into the left-wing back role.

Deploying Devenny's new club-mate Ethan Galbraith in a deeper midfield role is another option, one with the added benefit of getting the former Swansea City player on the ball with more frequency.

With Isaac Price sure to fill one of the more advanced midfield positions, using Galbraith elsewhere would then leave O'Neill with a decision to make regarding the slot beside the West Brom man.

Jamie Donley has started as a centre-forward in the side's past five games, scoring against Luxembourg and Wales since first being deployed as a nine, and it feels unlikely he would be moved into a deeper role now.

Patrick Kelly and Callum Marshall are options, but could O'Neill be tempted to throw an exciting but unproven attacking talent in at the deep end?

Liverpool's Kieran Morrison, spending the season on loan at Sheffield Wednesday, Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham of Everton, were all part of the squad in June with the former pair making their international bow in the friendly victory over Guinea.

O'Neill, who drew praise from Mikel Arteta during pre-season, also appeared off the bench against France four days later.

While competitive internationals would be a step up, Michael O'Neill has never been shy to give young players an opportunity before they have established themselves fully at club level.

Nobody connected with Northern Ireland will have fond memories of when the side last faced so congested a fixture list.

As a consequence of the Covid-19 pandemic, the June 2022 window similarly contained four games, with then manager Ian Baraclough presiding over losses to Greece and Kosovo, as well as a pair of draws with Cyprus.

Indeed, if not for an added-time equaliser from Jonny Evans against the Cypriots at Windsor Park, results would have been worse.

There is little doubt that such a schedule places greater demands on countries with fewer playing resources.

While, with everyone fit, there was a sense during the last Nations League campaign that O'Neill had settled upon his favoured starting XI, a trio of friendlies so far this year have given him the chance to assess further options.

In four games in 2026, O'Neill has used 27 players, including 21 in the game against Guinea alone.

Like Bradley, Sunderland's Daniel Ballard has not played for the side in this calendar year through injury, while the likes of Dion Charles, Bailey Peacock-Farrell and Jamal Lewis are among a group last selected in November 2025.

Approaching the four-year anniversary of his return to the job, it will be interesting to see whether O'Neill feels his first four-game window forces him to rely more heavily on the depth he has built across this year.

title: Jack Thorne warns some fellow scriptwriters are using AI ‘to cheat’
description: Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate...
fullText:
Adolescence co-writer criticises government inaction and calls for laws banning secret use of AI to generate scripts

Jack Thorne, one of Britain’s most successful screen and stage writers, has warned that some people in his profession are using AI “to cheat”, as he called for laws banning the secret use of the technology to generate scripts.

Thorne, who co-wrote the hit Netflix drama Adolescence and wrote the stage play Harry Potter and the Cursed Child, said that “writers need to be squeaky clean” in the face of AI models that “steal” the creative industry’s work.

In a wide-ranging speech in London, Thorne attacked government inaction over the AI industry’s mass-scraping of material to train their models. He said Keir Starmer’s government had been “a bit dazzled by tech” and lamented a failure to protect the copyright of writers.

However, he also said he had heard worrying stories about the misuse of AI among writers that risked undermining the profession.

“I have spoken to a number of execs and studio heads about their use of AI, and got hugely different responses, but what I did hear from them – and what anecdotally I’ve heard from a few writers close to me – is that some in my profession are using AI to cheat,” he said.

“What I’m not talking about here is using AI to help – to discuss things with, to check for spelling errors or help with layout. I’m talking about using AI as a replacement for endeavour, as a replacement for writing at all. Using prompts instead of writing words.

“That is, simply put, failing to write, they’re cheating their employers in doing so, and they’re cheating their fellow writers.”

Thorne, who is the president of the Writers’ Guild of Great Britain, warned that “if publishers, studios, streamers, can point to the writer as the problem, that gives them the excuse to behave however they’d like with content”.

He added: “Passing AI work off as your own needs to be unlawful. If you use AI to generate content and you do not declare it as such, then that is fraud and the companies you do it to should be entitled to prosecute you.

“To discourage it, the impact should be sizeable, and that requires laws but also us as an industry responding. Just as it should get you threatened with expulsion at university if you use it for essays, so it should have some professional impact on your career if you use it for text.”

Thorne said broadcasters such as the BBC and Channel 4 should threaten sanctions against those found to have used AI to generate their work.

“To protect the most vulnerable, it is essential,” he said. “As writers, what we are is what we make, and both the law and our industry should be absolutely crystal clear on that.”

Thorne also said AI must not be allowed to impersonate actors, directors and writers.

He criticised inaction by the government to protect the intellectual property of writers from AI models and said the way ministers acted in the next five years “will define what the next hundred years looks like for every writer in this country”.

Last year, Starmer’s government abandoned a proposal that would have required artists and copyright holders to actively opt out of having their material fed into AI systems, after a backlash. Ministers instead held a consultation on the issue.

“There are so many things the government could be doing,” Thorne said. “Crucially, observation without intervention for fear of upsetting their apple cart could be replaced by observation with intervention for fear of upsetting our apple cart.

“The pieces of AI we use cannot be built using thievery. Cannot be built on a copyright crime. That’s what government is there for, to set lines in an argument. While adaptation is probably necessary, legislating so that you are protecting us from the worst excesses is essential.”

He added: “This requires government leadership. In fact, it requires our government to take global leadership.”

A government spokesperson said: “Copyright laws must protect the UK’s position as a creative powerhouse while unlocking the extraordinary potential of AI-driven innovation. We are doing the work that’s required to get the right outcomes so both the creative and technical sectors can flourish in this country.”

title: 'Shades of Ferguson' as Neil runs show for Rangers
description: Peter Lovenrkands believes there were shades of Barry Ferguson in Dan Neil's performance on Sunday as Rangers stormed into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals at Celtic's expense.
fullText:
There were shades of Barry Ferguson in Dan Neil's performance on Sunday as Rangers stormed into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals at Celtic's expense.

That was the verdict of Ferguson's former team-mate at Ibrox, Peter Lovenkrands, who was blown away by the former Sunderland midfielder after he scored twice in the 3-0 win.

"Dan Neil ran the show from the start," Lovenkrands said on BBC Radio Scotland.

"On the ball he never lost a pass, simple things, he was doing everything right.

"I've not seen a performance like that since Barry Ferguson in the way he controlled the midfield."

The 24-year-old deservedly put Rangers in front on 23 minutes with a crisp low finish from the edge of the box and he capped off a fine team display with another emphatic finish late on.

"He popped up with goals, not just any goals, top-class finishes," Lovenkrands added. "It was an outstanding performance."

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

Rangers v Aberdeen & Edinburgh derby in League Cup semis

Neil signed a three-year deal at Ibrox in July and was immediately instilled as part of Derek McInnes' leadership group.

He once again wore the captain's armband in Lawrence Shankland's absence and rose to the occasion of his first Old Firm derby, excelling in the middle of the park alongside Nicolas Raskin and James Penrice, who inverted from left-back.

"Dan is going to get highlighted for his goals - two different types of finishes - but we knew we could occupy that space on the edge of the box if we attacked properly," manager McInnes said.

"You still need people to step up and show their quality and Dan did that. His performance was really strong as well, as was Nico and wee James in there.

"The three of them were terrific and it played a big part in us getting some sort of ascendancy in the game."

Neil has grown in stature in recent weeks, but this was his finest performance in a Rangers shirt to date, getting the better of proven performers Callum McGregor and Benjamin Nygren.

At one point, Neil spun McGregor and left the Celtic captain in his wake. It was reflective of Rangers' dominance throughout the 90 minutes and Neil's own excellent showing.

"It was a great team performance," Neil told Premier Sports. "We fully deserved the victory out there.

"In the last few games we've done well without the ball. Today we wanted to use the crowd and get after them - the lads executed it perfectly."

Neil was also quick to praise McInnes' pre-match team talk and how well prepared Rangers were for such a big game.

"We all believed in the plan," he said. "The gaffer is good before games and he made sure we were ready to run through brick walls.

"That togetherness and cohesion has really come on recently."

The teams meet again next Sunday in the Scottish Premiership, with Celtic hosting Ferencvaros on Thursday in the Europa League before Rangers travel to Celtic Park.

And McInnes is delighted by the "togetherness" his team is showing before another huge game.

"It's up to us to keep reinforcing the message that when you play at Rangers there's another big game round the corner and that's what we've got next Sunday," McInnes said.

"I love the togetherness, I need to have this team who cares for each other, has love for each other. When things aren't going well you sometimes see the true strength. We've had some soul searching and tough times the past few weeks.

"It gives so much encouragement to the club, fans, the board as to what we're capable of."

title: Time for Pocognoli to pick - who could be named in new-look Scotland squad?
description: Sebastien Pocognoli will name his first Scotland squad on Tuesday, but what can we expect? Will the new head coach use this clean slate as time to call upon new names? BBC Sport Scotland takes a look at the potential candidates...
fullText:
A new Scotland dawn is on the horizon.

On Tuesday, Sebastien Pocognoli will name his first squad since being appointed the national team's head coach for the upcoming Nations League B fixtures.

His predecessor, Steve Clarke, prioritised consistency in his squad during his successful seven-year reign, which ultimately culminated in a first men's World Cup appearance in 28 years.

But his loyalty was often viewed - from supporters at least - as his biggest downfall, with regular calls for fresh faces often unanswered.

Now, if ever, feels the time for such hopes to be heard.

But, will the Belgian make sweeping changes from the experienced squad who returned from the United States earlier than planned? Or will continuity be key for matches against Slovenia, Switzerland and North Macedonia?

The Tartan Army will certainly be hoping for the former, and BBC Scotland takes a look at some uncapped and out-of-the-frame players who could be in line for a call-up.

Irvine stays as Pocognoli refreshes Scotland staff

What awaits new Scotland head coach Pocognoli?

Youthful Pocognoli the brave choice for Scotland job

A problem area for the latter years of Clarke's reign will remain a problem area in the early Pocognoli days.

Angus Gunn started between the sticks at the World Cup and, though he has found more regular football in the States since joining San Jose Earthquakes, he has conceded a rather alarming 21 goals in nine Major League Soccer games - though he did make four decent stops in San Jose's win on Thursday.

He was joined at the major tournament by Craig Gordon - who has since retired from football - and Liam Kelly, who has not featured since Derek McInnes took over at Rangers in the summer, suggesting there could be two goalkeeping spots up for grabs in this squad.

Scott Bain could have felt a little hard done by not making the trip across the pond in June, given he was playing regular Scottish Premiership football with Falkirk and picked up his fourth cap against Ivory Coast in April.

He's made a steady start to his season - recovering from an error against Celtic to pulling off a string of impressive saves against Dundee United - with his Bairns boss John McGlynn recently tipping him to start for Scotland later this month.

Liam McFarlane may not be challenging him for a starting berth, but the 21-year-old must be well-placed for a call-up as the third-choice shotstopper.

Since joining Partick Thistle in the summer on loan from Hearts - after being stateside as the training goalkeeper in Clarke's World Cup squad - he has conceded just one goal in five Championship games and is well thought of by both club and country.

Given the sticky situation the Scots have found themselves in this department in recent times, surely including the youngster sooner rather than later with a look to the future is a step in the right direction.

Is Bain on course to be Scotland's number one?

Continuing on that theme, there could be a bit of a changing of the guard in the rest of the rearguard too.

Grant Hanley, 34, limped off in Hibernian's recent defeat by St Johnstone and John Souttar, 29, has not been included in any matchday squad for Rangers this term - amid interest from abroad.

Following his mighty impressive season on-loan at Motherwell last year, ex-Celtic centre-half Stephen Welsh has taken to life in England's Championship with Swansea like a duck to water, reigniting calls for his inclusion in the squad.

A former under-21s captain, the 26-year-old recently got the better of a fellow potential new cap in Stoke City's Luke Graham.

The former Dundee defender made the switch to The Potters after being involved in the A-squad's training before the World Cup and on the bench for the Curacao friendly.

Strong in the air and left-footed, Graham appears a direct competitor for Scott McKenna - as does Luis Binks.

Perhaps a more unfamiliar name, the 25-year-old captains Danish Superliga side Brondby and previously represented the Scots at under-18 level before playing for England youth.

In a fascinating and revealing interview, external last month - where he encouraged young Scottish players to remain in their homeland rather than become "a number" in England - the former Spurs youth product - who calls Aaron Hickey a pal from their Bologna days - spoke of his desire for a Scotland call-up, despite never having had that conversation with Clarke.

Since that article dropped in August, the clamour online for his inclusion has rocketed and it very much appears the ball is in Scotland - and Pocognoli's - court.

There has also been a fair bit of discourse surrounding Colby Donovan, who has been flung into Celtic's starting side in Alistair Johnston's absence - notably in front of World Cup squad member, Anthony Ralston.

It appears a matter of when, not if, the 20-year-old right-back will make the first team but he has stiff competition with fellow youngsters Hickey, Nathan Patterson and Max Johnston.

One could even throw in left-back Josh Doig to that pile too. The Sassuolo defender is another in line for a recall.

Returning from the knee injury he sustained on the eve of the Scots' flight to Florida, Billy Gilmour will almost certainly be included in Pocognoli's squad.

The midfielder lasted the duration of Napoli's opening Champions League match in the defeat by Arsenal last week, after coming off the bench against Inter Milan in Serie A days before.

His presence was missed stateside but hopes will be high for Gilmour to be at the heart of his country's next chapter.

Many thought Lennon Miller would take his seat on the plane, but Tyler Fletcher timed his run perfectly for that.

Things have not quite yet gone to plan for the 20-year-old at Udinese, as he struggles to break into the Serie A side's starting XI but with Scott McTominay recovering from heart surgery, the former Motherwell man might be given the chance to add to his four caps.

Hibernian's Josh Mulligan might also be in with a shout, despite his side's sticky start to the season.

Involved in the international set-up last year, the 23-year-old is yet to be capped but did impress in the Edinburgh derby Pocognoli attended earlier this month and has been one of the brightest and most consistent performers for David Gray's struggling Hibs side.

McTominay's heart procedure 'a complete success'

Speaking of struggles, Scotland still seem to lack that genuine, top class, goalscoring striker.

Che Adams appears to be a shoo-in - not least because he has two goals in three Serie A games for Torino - but who else joins him is a little less certain.

Rangers captain Lawrence Shankland is out injured, and at 30-years-old, Pocognoli now may feel the time to rely on Millwall's Lyndon Dykes is nearing an end.

Throughout the calendar year, there has been a real will-they, won't-they dance with Scotland and Oli McBurnie.

It appeared fairly clear under Clarke - who was unimpressed a private conversation between the pair was shared - that the Hull City striker would not be returning to his squad for the first time since 2021, but the Belgian may be willing to offer a clean slate.

Though he has not yet scored this season for the Tigers - who sit third in the Premier League - the towering and tough 30-year-old is their star striker and put in a tremendous performance as they mauled Manchester United, before setting up the second in their 2-2 draw with Chelsea at Stamford Bridge on Saturday.

Can Pocognoli afford to continue McBurnie's Scotland exile?

Is Sevilla's 'all-round striker' Ure ready to lead Scotland's attack?

While Scotland didn't spend nearly as much of their summer in the States as hoped, one Scotman's name certainly dominated the discourse during July and August: Robbie Ure.

The Rangers academy product was in demand across Europe after a free-scoring spell with Sirius in Sweden - 20 goals and three assists in 20 matches - and it resulted in a £5.5m move to La Liga giants Sevilla.

The 22-year-old has yet to put on his shooting boots in Spain but, given his eligibility for Ukraine, Pocognoli might be tempted to tie him down as soon as possible.

Also on the move in the summer was Kieron Bowie.

After his Hellas Verona side were relegated from Italy's top tier, he teamed up with Doig at Sassuolo and impressed, even before he opened his account in the dramatic victory over Juventus on Sunday - sparking wild scenes as he netted his second career goal against the Old Lady.

His attributes are clear. A strong, physical forward with a powerful left foot, he will be hopeful of adding to his two caps.

From on the continent to closer to home, there is a strong case Hearts head coach Wouter Vrancken’s preferred front three make this squad.

Leading the line is already-capped James Wilson, who appears a player reinvigorated following his loan spell with Tottenham Hotspur youths last season.

Another goal against Hibs - in front of the Belgian - ought to have done wonders for the teenager, who has started the season like a buoyant boy with something to prove.

He has been helped in no small part, though, by wide men Calvin Miller and Josh McPake.

The latter‘s goal at Easter Road sparked wild scenes in the away end as he announced himself as a serious contender for a call-up - if his performances in the Championship last year with title-winning St Johnstone were not convincing enough.

Another star who took his second-tier form into the top flight is Miller, who has - like McPake - immersed himself in the free-flowing football Pocognoli’s countryman Vrancken likes to play.

The clamour for the trio’s call-up is captivating, whether the new Scotland head coach pays attention to it, is another matter.

A big auld pool for Pocognoli to ponder from.

title: Benn unsure on future after defeat by Garcia
description: Conor Benn says he does not know what is next in his career after a crushing world title defeat by Ryan Garcia.
fullText:
Conor Benn says he does not know what is next in his career after a crushing world title defeat by Ryan Garcia.

The Briton was stopped in the second round on Saturday - only the second loss of his 10-year professional career - as American Garcia retained his WBC welterweight crown in Las Vegas.

Benn, 29, was fighting at welterweight for the first time in more than four years and had said the fight would be his last in the division.

"Everybody keeps asking 'what's next for Conor Benn? The truth is, I don't have the answer," he wrote on Instagram., external

"I've always wanted to be a servant of the public and give everything I have when it matters.

"But giving everything comes at a cost. And the people who have paid that cost more than anyone are my family and my kids.

"They've sacrificed time with their dad so I could chase this dream. They've had to share me with this sport their entire lives.

"So when people ask me what's next for Conor Benn, right now the answer is simple. Time with my kids."

Garcia reality check bursts Benn's bubble in Vegas

Benn, the WBC's number one contender, was outclassed by Garcia, who was making his first defence of the title.

Benn was taken to hospital after the fight, in what was understood to be a precautionary measure.

He turned professional with limited amateur experience, bypassed the traditional British, Commonwealth and European title path and built much of his reputation fighting against ageing former champions.

Benn said he planned to move up in weight regardless of Saturday's result.

The two defining nights of his career came at middleweight against Chris Eubank Jr, and a trilogy bout with Eubank remains a possible route back into the spotlight.

fullText:
Humans will have to compete with AI-powered virtual employees in the near future. Here are our tips for the last human holdouts

Futureproofing your career with an AI-resistant degree is a tough ask, says Charlie Ball, an expert on graduate employment for Jisc, the UK’s higher education digital, data and technology agency.

“What you’re trying to do is futureproof a 45-year career in a time of rapid technological change – and that’s really quite hard to do. What’s likely is that jobs that hinge a lot on human, face-to-face interaction are unlikely to be replaced.”

He warns however that the discussion should focus less on identifying specific vocational paths that are safe from AI, and more on how to equip young people with a suite of skills that allow them to adapt rapidly to labour market change.

But if pushed, areas of work that might offer more protection from AI than others include the following.

Research and development
Degrees in Stem subjects (science, technology, engineering and maths) have long been associated with good careers. Although AI will inevitably affect entry-level lab work, “the creativity and imaginative work will have to be done by humans,” says Ball. “The whole point of R&D is to find out new things, and AI can only really compare against stuff that it’s already got in its database.”

Engineering
We may see AI increasingly embedded in design and modelling, but human engineers will still be required to operate in physical, real-world environments that will continue to require human oversight. “Much of engineering is going to be hard to replace by AI,” Ball says. “We are likely still to need engineers to do the big stuff like civil engineering – building bridges and buildings. Those areas are likely to be OK.”

Creative arts and entertainment
“Although AI can produce creative art, people generally don’t like it very much,” is Ball’s verdict. He thinks we will get better at spotting its handiwork. “There will always be demand for human-led creativity. Everything AI currently produces is a remix of things that already exist. AI can’t create things. You’ll never get a distinctive new voice emerging. It can’t do that.”

Medicine
“We will still have doctors in 50 years’ time,” says Ball. “Their jobs will change somewhat. But people will want humans to deliver their health news, particularly the more difficult news. And no matter how good automation gets, when your kids are poorly, you will want to take them to a human GP.” AI can be helpful with diagnoses in some cases, “but it will still make mistakes. Where you will need someone to take responsibility for decisions, they will all have to be human.”

Nursing and midwifery
“AI and tech will get injected into many health roles, and on balance that’s probably quite a good thing, because at the moment we have nowhere near enough people doing these jobs,” says Ball. “But people will want humans to care for them when they are sick. People will want humans to look after them when they are old. I cannot envisage a situation where there will ever be a robot midwife.”

Education
“Nor are we going to get robot teachers,” he adds, despite the ongoing shortage of teachers in England. “There is already a role for technology in facilitating the delivery of education. But we will still want human educators to make this stuff relatable, and also for the pastoral side of student support. That will remain important.”

title: Bears, Bills and Ravens win on record-breaking Sunday
description: After kicking off the NFL season with a Super Bowl rematch and a trip to Australia, week one continued with a record-breaking Sunday.
fullText:
After kicking off the season with a Super Bowl rematch and a trip to Australia, week one continued with a record-breaking Sunday.

The Buffalo Bills and Baltimore Ravens showed why they are favourites to win the AFC Conference, and the Chicago Bears made a statement as they racked up 59 points.

Those wins contributed to an NFL record for the most points scored on the opening Sunday of the season since the league merger in 1970.

Here's what you need to know from the opening weekend.

The Bills changed their head coach in a bid to finally reach the Super Bowl with star quarterback Josh Allen, promoting offensive co-ordinator Joe Brady to the top job.

His first game was a big test, coming against last season's meanest defence, and the lead changed hands eight times in a thriller at the Houston Texans.

Running back David Montgomery scored three touchdowns on his Houston debut, but Allen ran in two touchdowns and passed for two more.

The 2024 season's Most Valuable Player was almost intercepted as he launched a hopeful pass into the endzone with less than two minutes remaining.

But on the next play 30-year-old Allen held his nerve with a 34-yard throw to Joshua Palmer that clinched a 36-31 win.

Buffalo's first five games are against potential Super Bowl contenders, so they needed to hit the ground running.

After missing last season's play-offs the Baltimore Ravens brought an end to John Harbaugh's 18-year tenure as head coach, and they made a flying start under successor Jesse Minter.

Zay Flowers, who became the NFL's fourth highest-paid wide receiver in the off-season, made five catches for a career-high 150 yards and a touchdown in the first half alone at the Indianapolis Colts.

Derrick Henry also scored twice before half-time to move into third on the all-time list for rushing touchdowns, then added another as the Ravens cruised to a 41-23 win.

But there was concern for Baltimore as Flowers and rookie receiver Ja'Kobi Lane missed the second half with hamstring and wrist injuries respectively.

The Ravens' impressive win was soon eclipsed by the Chicago Bears, who were level with the Carolina Panthers at 31-31 midway through the third quarter before romping to victory.

Running back D'Andre Swift finished with three touchdowns in a 59-37 road win - the highest-scoring week one game in NFL history and Chicago's highest score since 1980.

After leading the Bears to their first division title in seven years last season, head coach Ben Johnson has set some lofty targets.

"We want to be the highest scoring. We want to have the most wins. We want to win Super Bowls," he said.

Harbaugh is now in charge of a promising young roster at the New York Giants, and his first game came on a poignant night at the MetLife Stadium, which hosted the football World Cup final in July.

Two days after the 25th anniversary of 9/11, the Giants honoured New York's first responders and those impacted by the attacks with a series of tributes before Sunday's primetime game.

The Giants then produced a convincing 28-20 win over the Dallas Cowboys, with second-year quarterback Jaxson Dart passing for 230 yards and three touchdowns, while fit-again running back Cam Skattebo rushed for another.

It was a balanced team performance with a disciplined defence, a trademark of Harbaugh's team throughout his time in Baltimore.

With the New York Knicks ending their long wait for an NBA championship this year, there is genuine belief that the Giants can also get back in play-off contention.

The Arizona Cardinals have been tipped by many to finish with the NFL's worst record, while the Los Angeles Chargers are seen as play-off contenders.

But the Chargers were humbled on their own turf at SoFi Stadium, which will host Super Bowl 61 in February.

The Cardinals are trying to make a fresh start having brought in Mike LaFleur as head coach and released quarterback Kyler Murray, and they dominated possession in a 26-14 win.

Murray, who went on to earn the starting role with the Minnesota Vikings, made a wretched start at home to the Green Bay Packers, coached by LaFleur's older brother Matt.

Murray's first pass with the Vikings was intercepted, and the former first overall draft pick then suffered a concussion before being replaced by veteran Carson Wentz.

Despite falling 22-10 down late in the third quarter, the Vikings fought back to win 39-22, with Justin Jefferson claiming two well-taken touchdowns and a two-point conversion.

The Vikings have had nine starting quarterbacks since Jefferson was named offensive player of the year for 2022, and the wide receiver looked back to his best.

Although the Cincinnati Bengals have one of the NFL's most potent offences, they have been let down by their defence in the past three seasons.

The front office tried to remedy that in the off-season, and the revamped defence was impressive in their opener against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Three of last season's 11 defeats came despite scoring at least 34 points, and again the Bengals had little trouble scoring against the Bucs.

This time their defence did their job too, though, recording four sacks and forcing four fumbles. All four were recovered by Cincinnati, with one returned for a defensive touchdown in a 33-27 home win.

If the Bengals can maintain that consistency - and quarterback Joe Burrow avoids another injury-hit season - they could have realistic hope of returning to the Super Bowl, having played the last time the big game was held in LA in 2022.

title: 'Big Ludo' - trailblazing keeper who became West Ham cult figure
description: Ludek Miklosko, who has died aged 64, was a cult figure with West Ham supporters after his move to London in 1990.
fullText:
More than a quarter of a century after he stopped playing for West Ham, the chant still regularly sung by fans shows the affection in which former Hammers goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko is held.

I play in goal for West Ham (West Ham!),

Says "Oi! Big boy! What's your name?"

Miklosko announced late in 2024 that he was withdrawing from further cancer treatment three years after his diagnosis. Days later he returned to West Ham for a Premier League match against Liverpool to a hero's reception.

On Monday, it was announced he had died at the age of 64.

No matter that his birthplace of Prostejov is about 1,000 miles from Moscow (and actually nearer London), Miklosko was a popular player who went on a trailblazing journey and won 42 international caps - the last two for the Czech Republic following Czechoslovakia's dissolution.

In a pre-internet era, Miklosko was barely known outside his homeland when he arrived in the English capital from Czech club Banik Ostrava in February 1990 as a long-term replacement for Phil Parkes in West Ham's goal.

The fall of communism had opened a path for players to leave eastern Europe for the elite leagues in the west, and after a two-month wait for a work permit during which he trained alone, he eventually became the first footballer to move from Czechoslovakia to England.

Manager Lou Macari travelled to Prague to accompany his £300,000 signing on the flight to Heathrow Airport but missed his debut, resigning a day later, with Billy Bonds taking over.

Miklosko, then aged 28, began his time in England staying in a hotel, with little grasp of English and no car, and would be given lifts to and from training by team-mates Ian Bishop and Trevor Morley.

The goalkeeper went on to become a cult figure with supporters, making 374 appearances for the Hammers over eight years, and had a spell back at the club as goalkeeping coach after ending his playing days with a three-year stint at Queens Park Rangers.

He was named the Hammer of the Year as West Ham won promotion back to the top flight in 1991 with a squad that included Julian Dicks and Frank McAvennie, and appeared in FA Cup and League Cup semi-finals.

The 6ft 5in shot-stopper will be particularly remembered for some brilliant displays in front of the old Boleyn Ground crowd.

Most memorable of all was on the final day of the 1994-95 season, when he single-handedly kept out the attacking might of Manchester United to deny them a third consecutive Premier League title.

A victory for the visitors would have given them the trophy as Blackburn lost to Liverpool, but they were held to a 1-1 draw and Rovers were crowned champions.

Miklosko stood in United's way, denying Mark Hughes, Lee Sharpe and Andy Cole in what frustrated Red Devils manager Alex Ferguson described as a "siege".

Years later, the keeper visited Manchester United's training academy, where staff recalled his efforts.

"A few of them said: 'I was there and remember that game and I hated you'. We had a good laugh about it," he told West Ham's website in 2020, saying he "never tired" of talking about that match.

Miklosko had an operation to remove a lump he discovered on his hip in 2021, and while radiotherapy initially helped with a further stomach tumour, he decided against chemotherapy for more tumours after discussions with his doctors.

He had returned to Banik Ostrava as sporting director in 2022 and wanted to carry on working. Supporters there unveiled a giant banner in support of him at a game earlier in 2025, with his picture and the words 'Big Ludo'.

"I have two football clubs in my heart - Banik Ostrava and West Ham United - and in a funny way they are very similar. Even the mentality of the fans, very similar. Hard-working people, loyal and passionate," he said,

"If I am ever doing an interview here in the Czech Republic, I am always saying this and making this comparison.

"West Ham United is my second family. After all these years, they still remember me, still sing my name, and that is a great feeling."

His name is Ludek Miklosko. He will be fondly remembered.

title: Honda changes F1 design boss after slow start to return
description: Honda changes the leadership of its Formula 1 engine programme after the Japanese manufacturer's disappointing start to its return to the sport this season.
fullText:
Honda has changed the leadership of its Formula 1 engine programme after the Japanese manufacturer's disappointing start to its return to the sport this season.

Honda, who won four world titles with Red Bull and Max Verstappen from 2021-24, joined forces with Aston Martin as their works engine partner for 2026.

But the pair are 10th of 11 teams in the constructors' championship and have a best result of ninth for Fernando Alonso in the Dutch Grand Prix.

On Monday, Honda announced a new head of its engine development programme.

Yoichiro Fukao, the former deputy leader of the project, will become Large Project Leader of the F1 project.

He has replaced Tetsushi Kakuda, who has led power-unit development this season.

A statement said: "This organisational change is a planned transition designed to ensure the reliable transfer of technical expertise to the next generation of engineers.

"Following the introduction of the new regulations in 2026, and with further regulatory changes expected from 2027 onwards, Honda aims to establish a robust development framework and deliver a highly competitive PU by transitioning to the new structure at an early stage."

Honda introduced its first engine upgrade of the campaign at the Dutch Grand Prix.

But although head of trackside general manager Shintaro Orihara said Honda had "observed (a) step forward in terms of performance on our metrics", the step is said to have been small, and less than Aston Martin had expected.

The lack of performance of the Honda engine is said to be worth at least a second of lap time, adding up the losses from the performance of the internal combustion engine and the operation of the electrical system.

F1 engines in 2026 have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, and efficiency in energy recovery is paramount when the batteries are almost completely deploying and recharging several times a lap.

Alonso was 2.2 seconds off the fastest time of the session when he was eliminated in the first part of qualifying at last weekend's Spanish Grand Prix.

Honda's stuttering start to its official return to F1 is rooted in its tortuous route to the start of this season.

In October 2020, it announced that it was pulling out of F1 at the end of 2021.

Although Honda continued to supply engines to Red Bull on a more low-key basis until the end of 2025, only a small hub of engineers remained on the programme. The others were sent off to work in other parts of the company.

They remained competitive because development was frozen as part of the F1 rules from 2021-25.

When Honda decided in May 2023 to return to F1 in an official capacity for 2026, it set about rebuilding a team of development engineers, but did not bring back the ones who had produced the successful 2021 engine.

Instead, engineers with no experience of F1 were brought into the programme.

This season, it has started the process of bringing back the experienced engineers in the hope the programme can be accelerated.

For Alonso, this process has been especially painful, because he has already endured three difficult years of uncompetitive Honda engines with McLaren from 2015-17, when the company last returned to F1 after a hiatus.

This latest development comes as the veteran two-time champion has still not confirmed whether he will continue in F1 after the end of this season, when he is out of contract with Aston Martin.

title: European tech stocks hit six-week low as calls for AI slowdown worry investors – business live
description: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial...
fullText:
Good morning, and welcome to our rolling coverage of business, the financial markets and the world economy.

Investors are reassessing the value of companies driving the artificial intelligence revolution after several leading AI figures called for a slowdown in development for safety reasons.

Shares in AI-linked companies in Asia dropped when trading began today, dragging South Korea’s KOSPI index down by 3.7%. Chipmaker SK Hynix has slumped by 5.75%

SoftBank, a major AI invester, fell by as much as 13% in Tokyo after OpenAI’s chief executive officer Sam Altman said that the ChatGPT-maker won’t go public this year (SoftBank owns a stake in OpenAI).

Taipei’s Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company dropped by 1.2%.

Traders’ optimism about AI has taken a hit after the CEO of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down” – a call which was quickly backed by both Altman and Elon Musk.

Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless”, and warned that a swarm of AI agents could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet” in future.

Although Amodie’s claims have been disputed by some AI experts, investors are pricing in a slowdown to AI development which would make it harder for the industry to pay for its rapid rollout of data centres.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, says there is a “sour mood in the markets this morning”, explaining:

So if the AI race slows materially, the key question becomes: who pays for all that infrastructure? The leases, debt and power commitments remain even if expected compute demand and revenue growth slow. And that could bring credit risk increasingly into the AI story, particularly for highly leveraged data-centre operators and lenders exposed to projects built on aggressive assumptions about future AI demand, at a time when interest rates – hence borrowing costs – are expected to rise.

What’s interesting is that the slowdown may come not because Big Tech is out of cash, or because investors won’t play along. It comes from the actual people who develop these models.

fullText:
Big screen folder with slick software and advanced AI is just like a regular Android when closed

Google’s latest folding phone sticks with its tried and tested design of a traditional phone shape when closed and almost square when open, in the face of new competition from Apple’s squat iPhone fold.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is Google’s fourth-generation folder and is still one of the only models with a full water and dust resistance rating similar to standard slab phones. It costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799), which is £50 (€100/$100/A$100) more than last year as the pressure of RAMageddon continues to push up prices.

The 11 Pro Fold looks identical to previous models, but it is 19g lighter and fractionally slimmer in all directions with a slightly larger outside screen. Unlike Samsung’s slender Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra or squat models such as Apple’s iPhone Duo or the Galaxy Z Fold 8, the Pixel has the same ratio screen as Google’s slab phones and so handles precisely like them when shut with a bright and smooth 6.5in display.

Opened up, the internal screen is essentially square, which allows you to run two full-size apps side by side but is less ideal for video. The display is very bright, crisp and smooth, but the crease where it folds is more visible and detectable with your fingers than the best rivals. Like all foldable phones the screen is also delicate compared with standard hardened glass phones.

The back of the phone hides the excellent Qi2 magnetic charging and accessory support from last year, while Google’s gimmicky HiLight notification LED, as seen on the other Pro Pixels, replaces the camera’s flash.

Outside screen: 6.5in FHD+ 120Hz OLED (399ppi)

Inside screen: 8in 120Hz OLED (372ppi)

Camera: 48MP wide, 10.5MP ultrawide, 10.8MP 5x telephoto; two 10MP selfie cameras

Connectivity: 5G, eSim, USB-C, wifi 7, NFC, Bluetooth 6, UWB, Thread, GNSS

Water resistance: IP68 (1.5 metres for 30 minutes)

Dimensions folded: 155.2 x 76 x 10.1mm

Dimensions unfolded: 155.2 x 150.4 x 5mm

The 11 Pro Fold has the same Tensor G6 chip from the other Pixel 11 models with 16GB of memory, which works very well for all kinds of multitasking, remaining snappy and responsive with multiple apps on screen. It handles light gaming, but can’t match rivals for raw performance.

The battery life is a little shorter than last year’s model and rivals, lasting about 36 hours between charges when used on a mix of 5G and wifi with the screens in active use for about 2.5 hours each for browsing, messaging, apps and photos. Most will have to charge it nightly, but even on the heaviest of use days the Pixel managed to end the day without requiring a top-up.

The Fold runs the latest version of Android 17 with all of Google’s AI tools, including Gemini’s proactive system, the new supercharged voice dictation feature and six months of Google AI Pro subscription.

Many of Google’s more creative AI tools, including the Omni video creation tool, Circle to Search and Gemini’s information cards benefit from the larger internal screen. Google has made a number of modifications to Android to better fit the folding form, including a floating taskbar and a split-screen mode that can resize apps beyond the bounds of the physical display introduced last year.

The bubbles system, which was primarily used for messaging apps, has been revamped to allow as many as five apps of any kind to be opened as floating windows on top of a single or split-screen apps and minimised to a little taskbar. But it isn’t as flexible as Samsung’s true desktop-like floating window system that can be resized and placed anywhere on the screen.

The 11 Pro Fold will be supported until August 2033 with operating system and security updates, making it one of the longest supported devices available.

The battery is rated to last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity. The phone is repairable by Google and third-party shops, and self-repair with manuals and parts is due to be available.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold contains 24% recycled materials by weight. The company breaks down the phone’s environmental impact in its report and will recycle old devices for free.

The Pixel Fold has some of the best cameras on a foldable phone, including three on the back and two very good selfie cameras, one in each screen.

The rear cameras include a new 48MP main camera with a larger sensor, matching that in the regular Pixel 11, which captures better detail and has significantly better lowlight performance than its predecessor. The 10.5MP ultrawide camera is the same as last year and is still as solid this year. The 10.8MP 5x telephoto is also the same and shoots good photos that meaningfully reduce the distance to objects. It has a solid digital zoom that stretches up to 30x magnification, but not the generative AI zoom of the Pixel 11 Pro.

The Fold also has the new software features from the other Pixel 11 phones, including Camera Looks, which allows you to customise the processing of your photos for different styles. Magic Capture shoots video and photos automatically with one button, while the Creator suite helps you storyboard, trim and produce video content for social media.

The camera also has tricks to make use of the folding form, including modes to shoot when propped up and the excellent Made You Look feature that displays an animated character that reacts to your kid’s smiling to help take better photos.

Overall, the 11 Pro Fold has an excellent set of cameras that don’t feel a significant downgrade on top regular smartphones.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold costs from £1,799 (€1,999/$1,899/A$2,799).

For comparison, the Pixel 11 costs £879, Pixel 11 Pro costs £1,079, the Pixel 11 Pro XL costs £1,279, the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra costs £1,899, the iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Honor Magic V6 costs £1,499.99.

The Pixel 11 Pro Fold is a fairly minor hardware update for Google’s folding phone line, which makes it slightly lighter, smaller, brighter and faster, while keeping its overall look and feel the same.

It has great AI tools, slick software and some of the very best cameras. The inside screen is super bright and crisp, but the crease down the middle is more noticeable than rivals, the battery life is a bit short and it is thick and heavy compared to the best from rival Samsung.

As with all foldables the inside screen can be permanently marked by a fingernail if you press hard enough, so you must still be careful with it compared with a standard Pixel.

But if you want a folding phone to be exactly the same as a regular one when closed, the Pixel Fold is the one to get.

Pros: just like a regular Pixel when closed, good tablet screen, dust and water resistant, Qi2 magnetic accessory and charging, good performance, great cameras with 5x zoom, great software packed with cutting-edge AI, six months of Google AI Pro included, seven years of software updates.

Cons: very expensive, more fragile and costlier to repair than a regular Pixel, thick and heavy, cameras can’t match regular Pixel 11 Pro, battery life could be better.

title: How did the first Ultimate Championship go?
description: As the inaugural Ultimate Championship concludes, athletics has taken its first strides in a new direction.
fullText:
As poster boy Armand Duplantis performed the Ultimate Championship's official song and fireworks lit up the sky above the newly crowned winners, athletics had taken its first strides in a new direction.

Across three fast-paced evenings the inaugural event played out in Budapest, where a record $10m (£7.4m) prize pot was distributed among the sport's biggest stars.

It looked different. It felt different. And, after three successive sell-out crowds and positive feedback from the athletes, it appears it is here to stay.

"It's a good first step towards changing track and field for the better," said Usain Bolt, event ambassador and the greatest sprinter in history.

"The athletes are loving it. It's a different energy, a different vibe."

World Athletics and its president, Lord Coe, worked for three years to tackle the absence of a season-ending pinnacle event.

Rather than keeping to an established formula, the Ultimate Championship was a bold, innovative undertaking - and it is hoped it can exist as a testing ground to help shape the sport's future.

"We walked out, we came through the little starlights and we all looked at each other and said, 'this is unbelievable'," Britain's four-time global relay medallist Imani-Lara Lansiquot told BBC Sport.

"It's so rare that things really live up to the expectation, the hype. I'm so, so glad, having been in this sport for many years now, to actually see us be put on a platform and celebrated in this way."

Athletics has long grappled with the issue of maintaining the interest and excitement which it generates at the Olympics throughout the rest of those four-year cycles.

The structure of the season has not always been clear for occasional viewers, while showdowns between the world's top athletes can be inconsistent. From a storytelling perspective, that is far from ideal.

They are all issues World Athletics has sought to begin addressing with the biennial Ultimate Championship, while also compensating the athletes with record prize money.

The premise is accessible: condensed, fast-paced sessions, with the best competing against the best for a global title and significant prize money.

A striking new appearance and several innovative features ensured the Ultimate Championship provided a notably different feel to that of the sport's established global championships.

An infield painted black sought to focus attention on the illuminated live events, while the horizontal jumps were decided in a bright pink sandpit.

A new trophy waited for the winners on a plinth, with their crowning moment marked by sparklers and celebratory music.

New features for TV audiences attempted to enhance the viewer experience, with athlete headshots, win probabilities and projected finishing positions flashing up on screen.

They did so with varying success.

Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen was unimpressed by his predicted finishing position of 12th before winning the 5,000m title, while Britain's 1500m champion Josh Kerr was expected to finish last - a result of both athletes racing lightly over recent seasons.

There was a notable athlete-centric feel to the event beyond the increased financial rewards.

The world's top athletes arrived on the eve of the championship for a red carpet event featuring photoshoots.

Athlete videos were played inside the stadium before events and winners held centre-court style interviews before being escorted to a champions' enclosure, where they joined Bolt and master of ceremonies Noah Lyles.

On the videos, Britain's Georgia Hunter Bell said: "I do like the fact that it builds personality and character for, hopefully, people to connect with the athletes. That storytelling is something that's really interesting.

"If you think of superstars like Carlos Alcaraz, Serena Williams or Tadej Pogacar, obviously they're great athletes, but it's their personality coming through that makes it fun."

BBC commentator and former 1500m world champion Steve Cram said: "The key is the exposure of it. It's good for the sport. It's really good for the profile of the athletes."

But the championship did not avoid criticism - the biggest its exclusion of certain events.

World Athletics took the decision to include events based on viewer behaviour, including pulse rate and sweat response.

That meant that distance track events, including the 3,000m steeplechase and 10,000m, were omitted, while only selected field events were included. Shot-putters and discus throwers were excluded entirely.

The event format was also altered. Round progression in several field events meant increased jeopardy, with the competition whittled down to the top four athletes by the fourth and final round.

British long jumper Jazmin Sawyers told BBC Sport: "Some field events didn't get any attention because they're not here. The championship is worse off for not having them.

"It looks amazing in stadium and broadcast. It's dynamic. It's exciting. There's a place for it alongside regular championships.

"I don't think I would like to see it replace regular championships, but I like the idea that this is something that exists alone."

On the long jump competition format, she added: "I would love to see all eight [athletes] get all four jumps. It makes it more interesting.

"I was able to come from fourth to second. What if the person who was eighth could go from eighth to first? That's more exciting."

On the matter of the excluded events, Coe said the disciplines held at the Ultimate Championship were "not in tablets of stone".

Looking ahead to the next edition in 2028, the Ultimate Championship will be positioned at the end of a season which is headlined by an Olympics.

It remains to be seen how it will fit alongside the Diamond League - the sport's season-long series - in the schedule of the athletes.

Former Olympic heptathlon champion Denise Lewis told BBC Sport: "People have wanted to see something that looked different and felt like a different product. World Athletics has delivered.

"I don't think we know what it will do to the global calendar of athletics.

"The overall picture and the landscape isn't clear. There is place for this, but I do think it is unclear what yet."

Coe accepted before the weekend that there would be "no guarantee we're going get everything right" and said a "slightly different format" might be considered in future.

But, regardless, the competition was a statement of intent as the sport seeks to engage with new, bigger audiences while ensuring its star names are rewarded with prize money closer aligned to that of other sports.

Speaking after become Britain's first Ultimate champion in the 1500m, Josh Kerr said: "I welcome anything that can push this sport on to make it more entertaining for people to watch and athletes to go out and compete.

"There is one last thing that we can do to get it right and that is to let athletes wear their own brands versus their country.

"I love my country and competing for them, but we don't make money from that. We don't have the pay cheques other sports do just yet.

"My $30,000 pay cheque just came through from winning the World Indoors, so $150,000 is a huge jump and I'm massively appreciative."

title: Zverev turns US Open tears into triumph in transformational year
description: How a more composed Alexander Zverev stayed 'zen-like' to beat Ben Shelton and win the US Open, six years after a heart-breaking defeat in the final.
fullText:
As he stepped up to the baseline, Alexander Zverev could be forgiven for letting his mind slip back to the last time he served for the US Open title.

Six years ago, the German top seed threw away a two-set lead in a devastating loss to Dominic Thiem, having served for the match in the fifth set.

This time, instead of his own nerves, it was American Ben Shelton and the majority of the 24,000-strong crowd that stood in Zverev's way.

But this was a different Zverev: a Grand Slam champion now, having won the French Open in June.

Such was his focus that he did not initially realise he had sealed a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory.

After firing down another unstoppable serve to win the match, Zverev returned to the baseline ready to start the next point - only to be told by his team the match was over.

"In that moment I was in the zone a lot. I didn't hear noise at all," Zverev said.

"It's funny - tennis teachers always tell you to just play the next point and forget about the score.

"At that moment I forgot about the score and it helped me."

As the realisation sunk in, the 29-year-old broke into a broad and slightly surprised smile before raising his arms above his head.

It was a direct contrast to his defeat by Thiem in 2020, where a tearful Zverev said during the trophy presentation: "I wish one day I can bring the trophy home."

"We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now we've won two in three months," said Zverev.

"2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."

Zverev's parents were not there for his previous final at Flushing Meadows, but his father and coach Alexander senior was on the sidelines this time.

As well as paying tribute to his father, Zverev also thanked his mother for her support following his type 1 diabetes diagnosis as a child.

"When doctors tell you that life and sports will be very limited for that child, it takes a very strong mother to say 'my son will be whatever he wants to be'," Zverev said.

"My mother is the most important and strongest person I know."

Zverev caps transformational year with US Open triumph

All About US Open: Zverev claims second Grand Slam title

World number two Zverev has enjoyed his best year on the Tour, reaching the semi-finals at the Australian Open and the final at Wimbledon alongside his French Open and US Open successes.

He has been aided by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz, who swept the majors in the past two seasons, but a strengthened mentality and dedication to fitness has also helped.

"There is no-one as fit as Zverev, he is right up there," former Wimbledon champion Marion Bartoli said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"You can argue about Alcaraz and Sinner, and Novak [Djokovic] and Rafa [Nadal] when they were in their prime physically, but Zverev is right up there as one of the best athletes to play the sport."

Zverev was taken to five sets in his first two matches, with both finishing in the early hours of the New York morning.

He was two points from defeat in the first round, but rallied, played his way into form and did not drop a set from the third round until the final.

Faced with a partisan crowd against Shelton, Zverev did not buckle. He kept his emotions deliberately in check and, even though he lost the third set, never loosened his grip on the match.

"I'm so admiring of his strength of character and the zen-like state he's been in since the very beginning of the match," said former British number one Annabel Croft.

"The most extraordinary thing - and I don't think I've ever witnessed it - was that he didn't realise he had won.

"It was so bizarre, but it was like he was in a trance-like state while he was playing."

His serve - one of the best on the ATP Tour - was key against Shelton.

He won 39 of 42 points behind his first serve in the first two sets and did not face a break point until the middle of the third.

Shelton broke at the end of the third set to extend the match but the American made little impact in return games from then on, winning only four of 20 receiving points in set four

Victory means he will now have the world number one ranking in his sights - he trails Sinner by 1,810 points with two Masters 1000 events and the season-ending ATP Tour finals to come.

But Zverev is a polarising figure in tennis.

In October 2023, he was given a penalty order and fined 450,000 euros (£392,000) for bodily harm against his ex-partner, with whom he shares a child.

Zverev denied the claims and lodged an objection against the order. A trial in May 2024 was discontinued after a week and there was a separate settlement between Zverev and his ex-girlfriend.

At the time, the court told BBC Sport: "The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence."

Zverev was also accused in October 2020 of physical violence and controlling behaviour by another former girlfriend. He maintained his innocence from the start and there were no legal proceedings.

title: Former West Ham keeper Miklosko dies aged 64
description: Ludek Miklosko made almost 400 appearances for West Ham in the 1990s, and fans sang his name long after his exit.
fullText:
Former West Ham, QPR and Czech Republic goalkeeper Ludek Miklosko has died at the age of 64.

Miklosko made almost 400 appearances for the Hammers from 1990 to 1998 and was much loved by supporters, who regularly sang his name long after he left the club.

He later returned as a goalkeeping coach.

Miklosko withdrew from cancer treatment in December 2024, three years after his diagnosis.

Days later he returned to West Ham's London Stadium for a Premier League match against Liverpool to a hero's reception.

A West Ham statement read: "It is with deep and profound sadness that West Ham United announces the passing of legendary former goalkeeper and coach, Ludek Miklosko.

"Rest in peace Ludek, our beloved, inspirational goalkeeper and gentle giant of a man."

'Big Ludo' - trailblazing keeper who became West Ham cult figure

West Ham said a period of appreciation will be shown to Miklosko before kick-off in their Carabao Cup third-round match at Fulham on Tuesday.

They will also dedicate their next home Championship match, against QPR on 9 October, to Miklosko, who made 57 league appearances for QPR between 1998 and 2001 before retiring.

"We are heartbroken to announce the passing of my dad Ludek, following a brave and courageous battle with cancer," said Martin Miklosko.

"Dad simply loved West Ham United, and especially hearing his name sung loud and proud at every game.

"The club, and its fans, were and always will be a part of our family, so thank you all from the bottom of our hearts."

Miklosko won promotion to the old First Division with West Ham in 1990-91, his first full season with the club.

West Ham also reached the semi-finals of the FA Cup that season, with Miklosko winning the club's Hammer of the Year award.

He is best known for his performance on the final day of the 1994-95 season, when West Ham drew 1-1 with Manchester United when United required a win to finish top of the Premier League. The result meant Blackburn Rovers won the title.

When West Ham won the Conference League in 2023 in Prague, Miklosko was in attendance and was serenaded by fans while doing a lap of the pitch before kick-off.

Miklosko won 42 caps for the Czech Republic and former Czechoslovakia combined.

He ended his career as the head of the sports department at former club Banik Ostrava, where he spent eight years as a player before joining West Ham.
