fullText:
Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, called out a member of his own party for "intolerance and racism" in a social media post about University of Texas students.

Bo French, a Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, posted an image on X of a group of apparently non-White University of Texas football fans celebrating during the Longhorns' win against Ohio State on Sept. 12.

"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn't believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," French wrote in the post.

In his own X post, Cornyn wrote, "This is the Republican nominee for statewide office. Are other Republican elected officials going to condemn the intolerance and racism, or look the other way while it becomes normalized. This is how great political parties self-destruct. Sad."

Replying to another X user that criticized his post, French wrote that "I cheered the team for the win."

"But I weep for the families in Texas who can't get into UT because they prioritize foreigners over Texans. Shame on you for ignoring that fact."

In the 2025-26 school year, Texas residents accounted for more than 80% of students at the University of Texas at Austin, according to a release from the school. International students made up less than 10% of enrollment.

Trump says US could 'decide to stay' in Iran and 'keep the oil'

Cornyn, who was beaten in a May 26 primary by Trump-backed opponent Ken Paxton, the state's attorney general, has openly criticized his own party as his time in the Senate comes to a close. Paxton's Democratic opponent, state Rep. James Talarico, slammed the post as "blatant racism."

"Thank you @JohnCornyn for your leadership. Racism has no place in Texas. @KenPaxtonTX: will you condemn this blatant racism or will you cower to extremists?" Talarico said.

Texas House Speaker Dustin Burrows, a Republican, said that "you can oppose immigration policy without demeaning people because of their race and ethnicity," adding that French should delete his post.

French is a businessman, former chairman of the Tarrant County Republican Party and a first-time candidate on a statewide Republican ticket. That ticket includes Paxton in a tight race against Talarico as well as Gov. Greg Abbott who is seeking re-election against state Rep. Gina Hinojosa.

title: Woman dies of complications from measles in western Pennsylvania
description: NEW YORK, Sept 13 (Reuters) - The death toll in Pennsylvania's measles outbreak rose this weekend with a county coroner's ‌report of a woman's death from complications related to the ‌disease. The cor...
fullText:
NEW YORK, Sept 13 (Reuters) - The death toll in Pennsylvania's measles outbreak rose this weekend with a county coroner's ‌report of a woman's death from complications related to the ‌disease.

The coroner's office of western Pennsylvania's Jefferson County reported that a 40-year-old woman died on ​Saturday from complications associated with measles. The commonwealth has seen an outbreak of the highly-infectious disease, adding to a resurgence of measles in the United States as official data shows declining U.S. vaccination rates.

The coroner's office said it ‌was working with the Pennsylvania ⁠Department of Health.

"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a ⁠serious and potentially life-threatening disease," Coroner Greg Furlong said in a statement posted on Facebook.

The state Department of Health said on Friday that it has confirmed ​676 measles ​cases across Pennsylvania in 2026, with ​124 measles-related hospitalizations.

The first U.S. ‌measles-related deaths of the year were reported by the Pennsylvania Department of Health on August 25.

The Pennsylvania Department of Health said it is conducting its own review of the Jefferson County case based upon its detailed epidemiological case definition for a measles-associated death. That definition was provided to the ‌CDC and the Council of State and ​Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) on September 10, the statement ​added.

The CDC did not immediately ​respond to a request for comment on the Jefferson ‌County death.

U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. ​Kennedy Jr — a ​long-time skeptic of vaccines — asked his new CDC director to remove a reference to the two deaths from the agency's online measles ​tally after he questioned ‌whether the disease contributed to the fatalities, Reuters reported earlier this ​month, citing people familiar with the matter.

title: Ahead of Fed meeting, Trump says US should have world's lowest interest rate
description: DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) - No country should have lower interest rates than the U., President Donald Trump said on Sunday, days before the Federal Reserve's ‌next policy meeting.
fullText:
DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) - No country should have lower interest rates than the U.S., President Donald Trump said on Sunday, days before the Federal Reserve's ‌next policy meeting.

Speaking to reporters at the Irish Open golf tournament, Trump said he did not know ‌whether Fed policymakers will raise interest rates at their meeting this week. But he said the U.S. "should be paying the lowest interest rate in the ​world" no matter what the Federal Reserve's data indicates about inflation and the economy.

The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index, a key measure of underlying inflation, on Friday posted its largest increase in four months. That reinforced expectations that the U.S. central bank will raise the target range for its federal funds rate, now at 3.5% to 3.75%, at the conclusion of ‌its Federal Open Market Committee meeting on ⁠Wednesday.

Price pressures remain elevated as the economy deals with Trump's import tax increases and surging energy prices tied to the Iran war. Many at the Fed worry that the longer ⁠inflation remains high, the greater the cost will be to get it back to target.

The central bank's governors are meeting just weeks before midterm elections that will determine whether Republicans keep their slim majorities in both chambers of the U.S. Congress. A rate ​hike ​could add to voter concerns about affordability, according to recent Reuters/Ipsos polls.

Trump's ​approval ratings have fallen as inflation has persisted. ‌He has argued that the Fed's interest rate levels have helped other countries at the expense of the U.S.

"I know more about formulas than anybody, and with the best credit in the world, we make other countries rich," Trump said on Sunday.

The president, a frequent critic of former Fed Chair Jay Powell, has been more supportive of Fed leadership since his own pick for chair, Kevin Warsh, took charge earlier this year. But Trump recently has made his ‌demands more clear.

"LOWER THE RATE OR I'LL STOP TRADING WITH COUNTRIES ​WITH WHICH WE HAVE A DEFICIT," Trump posted on social media two ​weeks ago.

In additional remarks to reporters later on ​Sunday before he boarded a plane to return to the U.S., Trump reiterated that threat and ‌said: "We don't want to have deficits with nations. We ​want to have surpluses or ​at least break-evens."

Trump "will defend the independence of Kevin Warsh above all" no matter what the Fed does with interest rates, National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett told "Fox News Sunday."

But Hassett also underscored Trump's own preferences, saying that ​if the Fed raises rates, "I'm sure ‌he's not going to be super happy about it."

title: Adult woman dies of measles complications in growing Pennsylvania outbreak
description: A 40-year-old woman is the third measles-associated death in a fast-growing outbreak in Pennsylvania that’s sparked a political clash between state and federal officials.
fullText:
A 40-year-old woman who lived in Jefferson County, Pennsylvania, has died from measles complications, the county coroner confirmed Sunday. It's the third measles-associated death in a fast-growing outbreak that's sparked a political clash between state and federal officials.

The woman died Saturday, according to a news release from the Jefferson County Coroner's Office, which said it was working with the Pennsylvania Department of Health on the case. The woman hadn't been vaccinated against measles, the coroner, Greg Furlong, confirmed to CNN.

The death follows two measles-associated deaths reported in Lancaster County at the end of August, the first connected to the viral illness in the state in 35 years. That county is the epicenter of Pennsylvania's measles outbreak, which had reached 676 cases as of Friday, 108 of which were added in the previous week. One hundred twenty-four people have been hospitalized.

"This is a heartbreaking loss for the family and an unfortunate reminder that measles can be a serious and potentially life-threatening disease," Furlong said in a statement posted on the coroner's office's Facebook page.

The woman contracted measles after a family member had it as well, Furlong told CNN, and noted she also had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or COPD, and asthma, and had been on supplemental oxygen 24 hours a day before getting measles.

The state health department said it's in touch with the coroner and is conducting its own review of the case, and said it will provide the public with updated information when it becomes available.

In some of her first public comments about the country's measles outbreaks, Dr. Erica Schwartz, the newly confirmed director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, said in a statement that the agency hadn't been notified by Pennsylvania officials of the death.

"Despite repeated offers of assistance, Pennsylvania has not requested a CDC Epi-Aid, which would deploy epidemiologists and provide on-the-ground measles outbreak support," Schwartz's statement, shared with CNN by email, said.

"By contrast, Texas, South Carolina, Virginia, Kansas, New Mexico, and Wisconsin have officially requested CDC Epi-Aids and worked alongside federal teams to help bring their measles outbreaks under control. CDC remains ready to provide Epi-Aid support to Pennsylvania as soon as the state officially requests our help."

Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a Democrat, said in late August when the state announced the first two measles-associated deaths that he'd declined an offer from Robert F. Kennedy Jr., secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services, for federal help. He then said he'd told the secretary that his "actions and his rhetoric," including spreading misinformation about vaccines, was harming communities.

Kennedy, an outspoken vaccine skeptic, shot back on social media, accusing Shapiro of fearmongering and the "weaponization of infectious disease" for political gain. He suggested the deaths may have been "altogether fabricated" by one of Shapiro's "hopeful staffers" to support a narrative that measles infection is more dangerous than it actually is.

The two deaths in Lancaster County were in infants, the county coroner there said, but his office disputed whether one of the deaths was caused by measles. A newborn died of a ruptured spleen, which the coroner, Dr. Stephen Diamantoni, said his forensic pathologist deemed wasn't caused by the viral illness.

A second death, in a six-week-old infant with a serious genetic condition called Amish lethal microcephaly, was caused by measles, Diamantoni told CNN.

Measles typically causes about one in five people who aren't vaccinated to be hospitalized, according to the CDC. As many as one out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. One of every 1,000 kids with measles will develop brain swelling. The virus kills one to three of every 1,000 children who become infected.

"Many people associate measles with a childhood illness, but it can lead to severe complications in individuals of any age," Jefferson County Chief Deputy Coroner and Public Relations Officer Jason Stiver said in the office's statement. "Measles is highly contagious and can result in serious respiratory illness, hospitalization, and in rare cases like this, death."

The MMR vaccine is the best way to protect against measles, the CDC says. Two doses provide 97% protection against measles. Approved since 1963, the vaccine is very safe, and side effects are usually mild and go away on their own, the agency says.

In its statement Sunday, the state health department reiterated that last month, it "confirmed two measles-associated deaths in Pennsylvania," adding, "The Department's primary focus remains on stopping the spread of measles across the Commonwealth by expanding access to measles vaccination."

CNN's Brenda Goodman contributed to this report.

title: Election chaos in this red state just got even stranger for Republicans after Supreme Court ruling
description: The Supreme Court blocked Missouri's new congressional map, forcing the state to use 2022 boundaries that favor Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district.
fullText:
Republicans suffered a fresh blow in Missouri after the Supreme Court blocked a congressional map that could have helped the GOP gain another House seat in November.

The ruling, handed down last week, means Missouri will use its 2022 congressional map instead of the new boundaries backed by President Donald Trump and Missouri Republicans.

Missouri held its August primary under the new map, meaning candidates won their party nominations based on one set of district boundaries. But those boundaries will change before the November election, when Missouri is expected to return to its 2022 map.

Trump Dangles $5,000 Checks As Debt Surges — But Only If Gop Can Clear Major Midterm Hurdle

Typically, states redraw their congressional and state legislative districts once every decade after the Census to account for population changes and ensure that each district has roughly the same number of residents.

The new map would have shifted parts of Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver's Kansas City district into more Republican-leaning areas, making the seat more competitive.

Republicans hoped the changes would help them win seven of Missouri's eight House seats in the November midterm elections. The GOP currently holds six of the state's eight seats, while Democrats hold two.

Missouri must now use the 2022 map, which keeps Cleaver's district more favorable to Democrats.

The Supreme Court's decision came after more than a year of legal battles over which congressional map Missouri should use.

Missouri held its August primary under the new map, but the state will use its 2022 district boundaries for the November general election. That means some voters could be assigned to a different congressional district in November than the one in which they voted during the primary.

The change could affect more than 1 million voters, or nearly one-fourth of Missouri's electorate, according to an Associated Press estimate.

The conflicting court orders have added to the confusion, with the November election just weeks away. Candidates and election officials must now adjust to the 2022 boundaries.

Missouri High Court Blocks Gop-backed Congressional Maps Ahead Of Midterms; Trump Blasts 'Ridiculous' Ruling

The Supreme Court did not explain its reasoning in the brief order.

The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

title: Airman shot down in Iran shares harrowing rescue story
description: The American airman rescued from Iran after his aircraft was shot down in April shared for the first time details about the risky recovery operation.
fullText:
The American airman rescued from Iran after his aircraft was shot down in April shared for the first time details about the risky recovery operation during a "60 Minutes" interview Sunday.

"Bravo," the airman's mission call sign used during the broadcast to shield his identity, said his parachute was damaged after the plane was hit, and that during free fall, he did everything he could to "unfurl or pull pieces of the parachute loose."

"It was the most terrifying thing I've ever seen," he said. The fall broke his back, an arm and a shoulder, and left him with a sprained ankle and bloody scrapes to his head and face, he said.

Once he ejected from the F-15, the weapon systems officer managed to avoid detection by encroaching Iran forces, hiking up a 7,000-foot ridge with his injuries while equipped with little more than a pistol, a communication device and a tracking beacon, according to previous accounts by US officials and "Bravo's" account on Sunday. While the aircraft's pilot was rescued shortly after the crash, "Bravo" was rescued 50 hours later.

Both crew members have not been publicly identified by the Pentagon out of concern for their safety and as a safeguard against disclosing sensitive information.

"As soon as I found a spot that I felt provided some concealment, I started working toward communication," "Bravo" told CBS' Norah O'Donnell. "When I got to the moment where I could review and think about all that I'd gone through, I sent 'God is good,'" he added, describing the first message he sent.

CNN reported Saturday that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and political appointees in his department pushed for the two crew members to participate in the exclusively and highly publicized interview, according to multiple sources familiar with the matter.

Both airmen initially expressed reservations about doing so, while military officials were also wary of revealing classified details of the rescue effort, according to three of the sources. The pilot declined to take part in the interview. CNN also reported that political appointees within Hegseth's office insisted the interview go forward despite reservations voiced by the military's chain of command.

"This entire story is a complete lie," chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said when asked about CNN's reporting on plans for the segment.

"The decision to participate in the interview was each pilot's alone — because it is their story," he added. "As CNN notes, one pilot decided to participate and one did not. Additionally, the Department took great care to ensure operational security, sources, and methods were protected."

"Bravo" told CBS he hid alone in a mountain crevice for hours, while elite American service members, accompanied by US aircraft dropping bombs to clear the area, raced to locate the officer.

The rescue involved hundreds of American military and intelligence personnel, including special operations forces such as Army Delta Force and Navy SEAL Team Six. CIA operatives mounted a deception campaign beforehand to throw off Iran, whose leaders who had offered a bounty for the airman's capture.

The CBS broadcast featured declassified video from the Pentagon that showed elite Air Force pararescue operators making their way toward "Bravo" to rescue him. He declined to share what the service members said to him when they finally arrived.

The rescue featured some twists. The US military blew up two damaged MC-130J special operations transport aircraft that had been waiting to take the commandos and the rescued airman out of the country. But they had become damaged at some point during the operation and all 90-plus special operators were briefly stranded. After they were eventually rescued, the US opted to destroy the broken aircraft to prevent them from falling into Iranian hands and then send in new planes.

"Bravo" said the entire ordeal will stay with him. The moment he saw his rescuers arriving on the ridge line where he was hiding, he said, "was one of the greatest moments of my life, and I don't know how to say it any more clearly than 'thank you' for all that they did."

CNN's Zachary Cohen, Brian Stelter and Kevin Liptak contributed to this report.

title: Trump calls $5,000 payouts 'easy' to fit into federal budget

fullText:
NEW YORK/DOONBEG, Ireland, Sept 13 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump said on Sunday the United States can afford his promise to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult should ‌his Republican Party keep control of Congress in this year's elections.

"I don't know but it's easy if ‌the Republicans win. $5,000 to all adults in the country and we can easily handle that because we're taking in so much money," Trump ​told reporters when asked if Congress would need to approve the payments, adding that trillions of dollars were coming into the country.

Trump unveiled the idea of $5,000 payouts during a speech at the Republican Party convention last week. Speaking to reporters on Sunday in Ireland, where he was attending a golf tournament at his club in Doonbeg, the president said the U.S. ‌government has the funds to pay for ⁠it.

But any such payment would need to be approved by Congress, House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said on Sunday. "Of course, the devil's in the details. We have ⁠to figure all that out," Johnson told CNN's "State of the Union."

Democratic politicians on Sunday morning talk shows panned the idea, with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries telling ABC's "This Week" that it is not a "serious proposal."

U.S. Senator Mallory McMorrow, citing the elimination of some Affordable ​Care ​Act subsidies, cast doubt on whether the promised $5,000 checks would ​be sent even if Republicans retain control of ‌Congress.

"There was an ACA subsidy cancellation," McMorrow, a Michigan Democrat, said on CNN. "I think it was $1,000 we were supposed to get. So if you believe that you're going to get $5,000, I've got a bridge to sell you."

U.S. Representative Mike Lawler, a New York Republican in a closely contested race, would not specifically commit to Trump's $5,000 dividend proposal on Sunday.

"I support putting money back in the pockets of hardworking Americans," he said on ABC's "This Week," citing tax cuts ‌in the One Big Beautiful Bill that Republicans passed last ​year.

"But whether you call it a stimulus check or a dividend, the ​question is, how do you pay for it? ​That's my focus. We have a $4 trillion debt, and we have to be serious about ‌tackling that."

Lisa Gilbert, co-president of the consumer watchdog ​Public Citizen, earlier called the ​move an attempt to buy votes.

"This explicit and desperate attempt to buy votes in the November election is a new low. Trump knows he can't do this, and yet he's attempting to bribe voters with ​the false promise of cash to ‌help his party win an election, which is antithetical to every principle of American democracy."

title: New attacks in Hormuz and Saudi test nerves as war's spread worsens oil disruption
description: New strikes on Saudi Arabia and on ships in the Gulf tested nerves in the Middle East on Sunday, after an attack on a Saudi oil
fullText:
ADEN/DUBAI, Sept 13 (Reuters) - New strikes on Saudi Arabia and on ships in the Gulf tested nerves in the Middle East on Sunday, after an attack on a Saudi oil pipeline and an advance by Yemen's Houthis threatened to worsen the wartime disruption to global energy supplies.

Oil traders were expecting prices to rise again when markets reopen on Monday, following the weekend developments that jeopardise supplies from the world's ‌biggest exporter, Saudi Arabia.

The British maritime security agency UKMTO said on Sunday that a vessel had been struck by a projectile as it moved through the Strait of Hormuz, causing a fire and forcing the crew to be evacuated. Iran, ‌for its part, said one person was killed and four crew wounded aboard an Iranian commercial vessel struck off its coast.

In Saudi Arabia, state media released video of damage to homes and a mosque from the purported latest cross-border attack by the Houthis, in Jazan province in the south. The Houthis claimed separately to have ​struck a Saudi military base in a neighbouring province.

Southern Saudi cities have experienced regular alerts since last week, culminating in drone strikes on Friday that knocked out the 1,200-km (745-mile) east-west pipeline across the Arabian Peninsula that has served as the main route for global supplies of Middle East oil bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

That same day, the Houthis captured Perim Island, which lies in the middle of the Bab El-Mandeb, the "Gate of Tears" strait that controls the mouth of the Red Sea.

U.S. DIESEL HITS ANOTHER RECORD

Oil prices surged above $100 last week for the first time since July. The politically sensitive retail price of diesel fuel in the United States rose on Sunday to another all-time high above $6.20 a gallon.

Traders and Saudi oil buyers told Reuters on Sunday that Riyadh has enough oil stored at its Red Sea port of Yanbu to maintain ‌exports for just five to seven days if the pipeline struck on Friday remains shut.

After that, ⁠as much as 4% of global oil supply could be jeopardised, on top of the millions of barrels a day already lost to the disruption to traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

Saudi Arabia has not given full details of the extent of damage to the pipeline or said how long it will remain offline. Sources that spoke to Reuters have given conflicting estimates for the time needed to fix ⁠it, ranging from days to weeks. Satellite images have shown huge columns of smoke from locations along the pipeline.

After a quiet August when flows of Middle East oil trickled back up, the past two weeks have seen a steady escalation in the war that the United States and Israel launched six months ago. No peace talks have been held since an interim agreement in June collapsed after a few weeks.

In a rare diplomatic initiative, Iranian officials had said they would attend a meeting on Monday with Gulf Arab states in Oman to present an agreement they say ​has ​been reached with Oman governing future shipping routes through the strait.

But Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, posted late Sunday that the regional meeting had ​been postponed "in the interests of consensus."

"We remain committed to fostering dialogue that supports stability and lasting cooperation ‌in our region," he wrote in a post on X.

Iran's Fars news agency cited an Iranian foreign ministry official on Sunday evening as saying that the Oman meeting was postponed at the request of some regional countries in a decision jointly made by Tehran and Muscat. The official said Iran would coordinate with Oman to determine a suitable date for holding the meeting, the agency said.

Iraq had said it would send a delegation, and a Gulf official had told Reuters that Saudi Arabia and Qatar would be represented by their foreign ministers.

A senior Iranian official had told Reuters on Saturday that officials would discuss Hormuz and other issues at the meeting, but added it would probably not yield a signed agreement to reopen the strait. Bahrain said it would not meet with any Iranians.

In an interview with London-based pan-Arab news outlet Al-Arabi Al-Jadeed, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said despite any agreement with Oman, Iran would not reopen the strait until the United States satisfies Tehran's demands.

HOUTHI ADVANCES POSE NEW DILEMMA FOR WASHINGTON

The U.S. has so far failed to achieve the ‌objectives President Donald Trump set out when he launched "Operation Epic Fury" in February: to end Iran's nuclear programme, prevent it from being able to attack ​its neighbours and create conditions for its people to topple their rulers.

Iran, having withstood the superpower onslaught despite military and economic losses, hopes to emerge stronger ​than before the war, including with the newfound power to collect fees from ships that use the strait.

The attacks on ​Saudi Arabia and the Houthi advances in Yemen pose a new dilemma for Washington, which wants to support its Saudi allies and protect shipping but is wary of joining war on another front. The Houthi attacks ‌have also left Gulf states with a difficult choice: accept growing economic pain or engage with ​Iran.

The Houthis, mountain fighters who captured Yemen's capital in 2014, have been ​battling a Saudi-led coalition for more than a decade but had mostly kept out of the wider Middle East war until recent weeks. Their advance along the Red Sea coast is part of the biggest eruption of fighting in Yemen for years.

The United States bombed the Houthis for two months in 2025, but Trump halted that campaign after announcing the group had lifted a threat to attack Red Sea shipping.

Three sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince ​Mohammed bin Salman, phoned Trump on Thursday asking for military aid to fight the Houthis, but ‌was offered only intelligence support for now.

Trump acknowledged on Saturday that he had spoken to the crown prince, and said the Houthis had also phoned the U.S. administration, asking Washington to keep out of the Yemen war.

title: Houthis enter US 'kill box' after seizing Red Sea 'cork,' former Pentagon official warns
description: Houthi rebels seized Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, but a former Pentagon official warns they've entered a vulnerable U.S. Navy kill box.
fullText:
Iran-backed Houthi rebels captured Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait Sept. 11, opening a new front at a vital global shipping chokepoint as a former Pentagon official warned Sunday the militants had entered a "kill box."

The island's capture came after a month-long offensive along Yemen's western coast that killed more than 1,500 soldiers and forced Yemen's government to acknowledge a "painful" defeat, according to The Associated Press.

"With Perim, they have gained what we could call the cork in the Red Sea bottle," Morgan Murphy, a former Pentagon press secretary and retired Navy captain, told Fox News Digital.

"But they've put themselves into a kill box. They're nowhere near the capability of the United States and if the president so chooses, he can wipe them off the face of that rock pretty easily," Murphy warned.

Saudi Arabia Tells Trump Now Is The Time For Military Action As Iran-backed Houthis Advance

Despite Perim sitting in the middle of the narrow maritime passage, Murphy detailed how the Houthis had effectively placed themselves in an area that is vulnerable to concentrated fire.

"Perim cuts that chokepoint right in half, and it's only 18 miles wide there," Murphy said.

He said the island has served as a pivotal maritime vantage point for hundreds of years, previously targeted for control by French forces and held by the British Empire for over a century.

Perim — a desolate volcanic island also known as Mayun — also sits roughly 20 miles off the Horn of Africa, placing it in proximity to Camp Lemonnier in Djibouti, home to one of the largest U.S. military installations on the continent.

"We have incredible firepower in that region, and that's a little rock in the middle of that strait. It's a volcanic rock. It doesn't have any water. It's uninhabitable," Murphy warned.

"There's no vegetation to speak of. And the Houthis have just massed their troops on that rock. So what that is, what we would call that in the Navy, is a kill box."

Satellite imagery of the island shows a 1.85-kilometer (6,070-foot) runway alongside three military hangars, which regional intelligence reports attribute to past construction by the United Arab Emirates.

"There's a 6,000-foot airstrip on that island. I think that Emiratis built it," Murphy said.

'Gate Of Tears' At Risk: Iran Threatens Major New Global Chokepoint If Us Moves On Hormuz

"It's nice to have an airstrip, and especially a long runway, but we don't know the condition of that runway. We don't know how they could possibly use that runway, and they certainly don't have the sophisticated air power that the United States and its allies have to project power from that runway."

He added that the U.S. military holds overwhelming force options if commanders elect to target the island.

"We could wipe that rock into glass, just blast it into a smooth glass surface, put skates back on our feet, and skate all over it," Murphy said.

"That's why the Houthis have kind of played coy with the president, and they know that even if they fortify that rock they're not going to be able to hold it in the face of the United States Navy."

The developments come amid diplomatic maneuvering between Washington, Riyadh and the Houthis in recent days.

Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had called President Donald Trump twice Sept. 10 to urge him to authorize U.S. military strikes against Houthi positions.

Trump declined direct intervention, with U.S. officials noting the administration has no immediate plans for direct combat involvement but will continue offering intelligence assistance.

Iran And Houthi Terror Proxy Facing Red Sea Threat From Pro-us African Nation

Speaking to reporters in Dublin on Sept. 12, Trump also indicated the Houthis had signaled a desire to avoid direct confrontation with American forces.

"The Houthis called us, and they don't want to fight with us. They let us know, they don't want to fight with us... they don't want us to go after them," Trump said.

Murphy suggested, however, that Washington's restraint should not be mistaken for inaction.

"I can't speak for the president. But this administration has not shown a lack of resolve to use force," Murphy said.

"I wouldn't doubt at all if the president took steps to pound some of these folks into the sand if they continue to really disrupt the global energy supply."

Yemeni government, regional and Iranian sources told Reuters the Houthi advance was sustained by Iranian weaponry and tactical direction from the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC, with U.S. officials estimating hundreds of IRGC officers remain active in Yemen.

Murphy noted that Tehran's strategy appears designed to drive up global fuel prices by choking critical shipping lanes.

Trump Threatens 'Major Military Punishment' For Iran Over Future Houthi Attacks

Comparing the conflict to historical naval power struggles, Murphy emphasized the strategic mismatch.

"We're in a different era. They are nowhere near the sophistication of the world's major powers. The Houthis are using a 19th-century playbook. They are not using 21st-century warfare," he said.

"So, yes, they've caught a critical cork in the Red Sea bottle, but how they use it remains to be seen," Murphy concluded.

"This is an example of why great powers really have to have a strong Navy. This is why Great Britain had a strong navy. This is why the United States has a strong navy, because there's so many regional powers who want to try to bottle up shipping, whether it is in the Strait of Malacca, whether it is in the Strait of Hormuz, and here, in this case, in the Red Sea."

"I think what we're going to see in the next several days and weeks is a coordinated effort by the Trump administration to make sure our allies are on board in helping us keep these critical waterways open, free, and clear for freedom of navigation," he said.

title: Arrest rips apart media narrative on death of Black woman found hanging from Mississippi tree
description: Jarques Ratliff faces a murder charge in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old mother found hanging from a tree behind a Jackson, Mississippi home.
fullText:
Mississippi authorities have arrested a 51-year-old man on a murder charge after an official homicide ruling in the death of Tasia Fortune, a 29-year-old Black mother of four found hanging from a tree behind an abandoned home last month.

The arrest follows weeks of intense media attention and widespread online discussion regarding the circumstances surrounding Fortune's death in a state with a historic legacy of racialized violence. But law enforcement officials confirmed that the suspect taken into custody is Jarques Ratliff, a Black Jackson resident who had a prior personal connection with Fortune.

Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney announced during a news conference Saturday that Ratliff was taken into custody without incident while walking along Capitol Street in Jackson, shortly after officers executed search warrants at related properties.

Aoc's 'Modern-day Lynchings' Claim Torn To Shreds Online As Black Hanging Case Findings Tell A Different Story

Chief Brackney emphasized that while the arrest marks a significant breakthrough, the investigation remains active and additional arrest warrants are expected to be served as detectives follow further leads.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., last week warned of "racial terror" and "widespread modern-day lynchings" in the U.S. as she joined dozens of Democrats demanding that the Department of Justice investigate hanging deaths of Black Americans.

Fortune's body was discovered Aug. 3 in the backyard of a vacant property in the 500 block of Road of Remembrance in Jackson.

Although investigators logged hundreds of hours interviewing nearly 15 individuals and reviewing physical evidence over the past month, formal arrest warrants could not be executed until the Mississippi State Medical Examiner's Office officially classified Fortune's death a homicide late Thursday.

Once that classification was handed down, members of the Jackson Police Department's robbery-homicide unit moved swiftly to secure and execute two search warrants alongside the arrest warrant for Ratliff.

Addressing public interest in the case, Chief Brackney acknowledged the heightened scrutiny but stressed that law enforcement remains strictly guided by verifiable physical evidence rather than external speculation. She noted that authorities understood public concern given Mississippi's history but said the department is bound to ensure all public statements are backed by forensic facts.

"We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe and across the community. We understand the questions and the desire for answers given Mississippi's history," Brackney said.

"We understand this case is being viewed through a broader lens — a global lens — and we do not dismiss those concerns. We are taking them seriously. At the same time, we do have a responsibility to make sure that what we say publicly is supported by our evidence and the facts."

Brackney also directly clarified that law enforcement had never officially designated any persons of interest prior to Ratliff's arrest, refuting social media reports that a 65-year-old man had previously been identified as a suspect.

Cops Drop Murder Probe After Coroner Rules Man's Bloody Stabbing Death Was Freak Accident

Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey, said police promptly notified her family of the homicide ruling and Ratliff's arrest on Friday. Spivey expressed gratitude for the police work and reiterated her firm belief that her daughter did not die by suicide, adding that Fortune would never take her own life.

According to family members and an online obituary published in Kentucky, Fortune grew up in Kentucky, skipped her junior year of high school and was a star cross-country runner guided by strong religious faith before relocating to Jackson a decade ago.

Spivey noted that her daughter had experienced homelessness in recent years but was actively working to launch a cleaning business and stabilize her life prior to her death.

Ratliff is being held at the Hinds County Detention Center on a charge of murder. According to Mississippi State Defender André de Gruy, Ratliff is scheduled to make his initial appearance in Jackson Municipal Court no later than Monday morning, where formal charges will be read and bond conditions set.

Police have not publicly detailed the specific physical evidence linking Ratliff to the scene, nor have they expanded on the exact nature of his personal association with Fortune as investigators prepare for further potential arrests.

title: From struggling to walk to lifting trophy - how Rybakina triumphed
description: Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.
fullText:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York unable to walk without pain after injuring her foot. She leaves the city as the US Open champion and new world number one.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina produced a brilliant performance to beat two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4 5-7 6-2 in Saturday's final and repeat her Australian Open success against the same player in January.

Clutching the trophy on Saturday night, Rybakina reflected that "some magic is happening" for her after her difficult lead-in to the tournament.

The 27-year-old aggravated a foot injury during her quarter-final in Cincinnati against Iga Swiatek last month, a little over a week before the final major of the year began.

Playing on through injury could have had dire consequences for the rest of her season - but Rybakina, knowing the top ranking was in her grasp, wanted to try to play in the final Grand Slam of the year.

"I was so upset. I didn't know actually how it was going to be day by day," she said.

"We arrived in New York and did an MRI. It didn't look that great.

"I couldn't even walk for the next few days without pain.

"I was lucky enough to have a very good doctor in Australia. She was on the phone with us all the time and somehow, with the team, we made a plan."

Rybakina did not do any on-court training for a week, but daily recovery sessions in the gym - plus trips for dinner and to the cinema to "switch the mind" - helped get her ready for another major triumph.

She won her first four matches at Flushing Meadows without dropping a set, including seeing off four-time major winner Naomi Osaka.

Her run from then on - which included beating Olympic champion Zheng Qinwen in the quarter-finals, outlasting third seed Coco Gauff in the semis and outplaying top seed Sabalenka in the final - was nothing short of outstanding.

"I was so unlucky with the injury, but I'm very proud," Rybakina said.

'Tough to control emotions' as Sabalenka suffers another near-miss

Rybakina wins US Open to inflict further pain on Sabalenka

Listen: US Open podcast - Rybakina crowned champion

Rybakina had already been confirmed as world number one by reaching the semi-finals in New York. The fact that her final opponent was Sabalenka, the player she will replace at the top of the rankings, added an extra dimension to Saturday's championship match.

Rybakina won the first set despite her serve, one of her biggest weapons, misfiring.

She landed only 27% of her first serves during the opener, but still won 22 of 30 points behind her serve and did not face a break point as she took the lead.

Sabalenka eventually broke in the 12th game of the second set to send their match the distance, but it was Rybakina who dominated the decider.

While her Belarusian opponent grew visibly more frustrated as the final slipped away, Rybakina remained remarkably composed.

"The way she [Rybakina] quietly walks around, she doesn't really lift her head up and she gives no emotion away whatsoever," former British number one Annabel Croft said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Rybakina is like a machine out there. You never know what's going on in her head."

However, nerves did show when Rybakina threw in two double faults as she served for the title.

At 40-30, the trophy in her sights, Rybakina could have blinked. Instead, she coolly sent down her 12th ace of the match to secure her third Grand Slam title.

The second seed produced her biggest celebration of her three major wins - a smile and both arms raised in celebration as she took in the applause.

Rybakina has now won two of her three Grand Slam finals against Sabalenka, all of which have come on their favoured hard courts.

On Monday, Rybakina will become the 30th different women to top the world rankings.

She is a different personality to Sabalenka, who held the position for the past 99 weeks, but Croft believes she will "take it in her stride".

"I actually think she has the right personality to deal with it," Croft said.

"There are going to be a lot of players around her nipping at her heels. She can fluctuate with her levels, but when it really matters, we've seen her be able to bring it to the table.

"It's not going to be easy to hang on to it. I think women's tennis is really exciting right now."

Rybakina has completed three parts of the career Grand Slam, with just a French Open victory missing from her collection.

After winning Wimbledon in 2022, she did not claim her second major until January's Australian Open, and has now added a third in New York.

She has never previously been further than the quarter-finals at Roland Garros, although she did win a WTA 1,000 event on clay in Rome in 2023.

Former British number one Laura Robson said on Sky Sports: "She is an all-surface player - clay is the worst one, but when you get her on something that's quite lively or quick, she's unplayable at times.

"I genuinely think she will win many more Slams. I just don't see, when her serve and return are on, how pretty much anyone can beat her on a hard court."

title: Boks power & All Blacks of old - what did we learn from series?
description: What did we learn from South Africa's Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series victory over New Zealand?
fullText:
South Africa further cemented themselves as the world's best team with a 3-1 victory over New Zealand in the Rugby's Greatest Rivalry series.

After losing the opening Test in Johannesburg, the world champions won three straight games, comfortably claiming the series with a 43-28 win in Baltimore.

The fourth Test, played in the United States, came after three Tests in South Africa where the All Blacks continued to show promising signs under Dave Rennie.

With the Rugby World Cup next year, what did we learn from the series, which replaced this year's Rugby Championship and will be played again in 2029?

New Zealander Tony Brown's arrival as attack coach in 2024 pointed to South Africa's ambition to dominate in all facets of the game.

The former Highlanders head coach, who will join the All Blacks in 2028, is known for creating a cohesive attacking shape built on sharp ball movement.

But having been outscored in terms of tries over the first two Tests, the Springboks flipped their pack-power trump card - pivotal to their back-to-back World Cup successes - to prevent a repeat of New Zealand's victorious 1996 series win in South Africa.

Nothing illustrated that more than a monster maul that started just inside New Zealand's 22 and ended with Malcolm Marx peeling off to score the decisive try under the posts.

That came after a penalty try from a scrum in the first half. In Baltimore, their power again proved too much.

"South Africa have tried to play expansively a couple of times when we have dominance after hurting teams in the maul or scrum," Schalk Brits, a 2019 World Cup winner, told BBC Sport.

"New Zealand didn't have that dominance in the forwards, but people said they played beautiful rugby. I don't care if it is beautiful or not.

"Beauty is in the eye of the beholder and I love a maul and scrum."

Fly-half Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, who was injured at the end of May, returned to start all four Tests. He was initially named on the bench for the second match, only for Handre Pollard to withdraw.

Despite improving as the series went on, the 24-year-old lacked his usual flashes of individual brilliance.

It remains to be seen whether South Africa turn back to 32-year-old Pollard, as they did in 2023, on the biggest occasions to close out games.

Rassie Erasmus' experienced back-to-back World Cup winners - Marx (32), Eben Etzebeth (34), Pieter-Steph du Toit (34), Siya Kolisi (35), Damian de Allende (34), Cheslin Kolbe (32) - all remain regular starters.

The world champions have proven they can also play an exciting brand of attacking rugby, but appeasing the masses will not matter if a familiar formula can bring them three straight World Cups.

Scott Robertson's dismissal in January after two years as head coach sunk New Zealand to a new low.

Rennie, not the flashiest appointment, had to hit the ground running, and a stunning Test win over South Africa at Ellis Park was a case of doing just that.

The 33-16 victory injected jeopardy into a series which many had the Springboks winning comfortably, given their home advantage and recent dominance.

Hurricanes half-backs Cam Roigard and Ruben Love, both aged 25, were trusted by Rennie to instil a return to the All Blacks way - the ability to score from transition from anywhere on the field and compound scoreboard pressure.

Four or more tries in each Test in South Africa showed just that, with the third Test all square at half-time.

"Scott Robertson was a good culture coach but maybe not a brilliant technical coach. Dave Rennie is a brilliant technical coach," former England wing Ugo Monye told Rugby Union Weekly.

"After the Nations Championship, you could see the structures and how they want to play. I think the All Blacks' backline is the most skilled in World Rugby."

Love struggled to have the same commanding impact in Tests two and three, with fly-half Richie Mo'unga returning for the Baltimore game, his first Test since the World Cup final.

The 32-year-old Mo'unga, who is back after a stint in Japan, was not at the standard that made him one of the best fly-halves at the 2023 World Cup.

However, getting him back up to speed will be an All Blacks goal over the next 12 months.

Former England scrum-half Danny Care said: "Imagine what New Zealand would do with a platform and some dominance. It is great for the game that they are coming back to be the All Blacks of old, and the next 12 months will be fascinating."

South Africa live for must-win games. That is when, according to Brits, the Boks "come alive".

Defeat at Ellis Park cost them their world number one status - which was quickly regained - but also exposed a vulnerability.

South Africa, who lost matches in the pool stages of the past two World Cups, are currently the favourites to win next year's tournament in Australia, bringing a pressure they have not experienced previously.

"We hate being the favourite, we almost have to have our backs against the wall," Brits said.

"We prefer not to have the eyes on us and move under the radar. I think that is the best way for any team."

Back-to-back Six Nations champions France sent a weakened side to Christchurch in July and lost 34-32 to New Zealand.

When matched against the Springboks last November, France were beaten emphatically, 32-17.

Brits believes France are "the most settled" and offer tactical flexibility similar to that of the world champions.

"I feel like South Africa have an advantage as they can play multiple styles, and it feels like most other nations don't have that capability," Brits said.

"The only team that can play multiple styles is France, as they can grind it out with the forwards, play the kicking game and the expansive game as well."

He added that England still need to become what they are "supposed to be" and to keep an eye on Ireland, who are travelling "under the radar" after peaking in previous World Cup cycles prior to the tournament.

"Ireland still have amazing rugby players and coaches – the best coaches out there - and a top-four squad," Brits added. "Be careful of Ireland."

description: England's Ali Carter wins the English Open in style with a 9-6 victory over Mark Williams in front of his home support in Brentwood.
fullText:
England's Ali Carter won the English Open in style with a 9-6 victory over Mark Williams in front of his home support in Brentwood.

Essex-born Carter, 47, won all-but one frame in a dominant evening session, sealing the last frame without reply to claim the winner's prize of £100,000.

Neither player had previously won the English Open, and it was Wales' Williams who took control to lead 5-3 at the interval.

However, Carter won the first two frames after the resumption to level and from there never trailed.

"I thought, 'I am going for this'. I didn't care where the balls were today; I wasn't going to lose this by turning down balls," Carter told TNT Sports.

"I kept potting the big shots and knocking all the difficult balls in. I am delighted.

Carter, who has Crohns disease and twice fought cancer – most recently being given the all-clear in 2014 having been diagnosed with a cancerous tumour on his lung – added: "I have been to hell and back.

"I know I am not everyone's cup of tea, but what you see is what you get."

The victory, a seventh ranking title of his career and first since 2024, also moves Carter back into the world's top 16, moving up nine places from 25th.

"It is a great achievement to pick up another trophy at 47, especially in front of my home fans," he said.

title: Intelligence & resilience key in statement win for Maresca's Man City - Murphy
description: Match of the Day pundit Danny Murphy explains how Manchester City beat Manchester United at Old Trafford despite being down to 10 men for most of the game.
fullText:
If you go to Old Trafford in a derby, go down to 10 men in the first 25 minutes and still come away with a 1-0 victory, it tells you a lot about your players.

Sunday's result was a statement win for Manchester City's new manager Enzo Maresca, who got his tactics spot on, but his team's performance will have showed him exactly what they are about.

I am talking about the mentality, discipline, organisation and energy you need in order to get a result when things go wrong for you like that in a game.

They were smart too, and that experience and ability not to panic goes a long way in football in situations like the one City faced following Phil Foden's early red card.

City are used to always having most of the ball but they were fine without it against United. That is down to leadership and communication - not just from the manager, but from the players on the field.

Maresca deserves plenty of credit for his decisions too, but he must be thinking he is a lucky man for having the group of players he does, because their intelligence and resilience was key.

As I said on Match of the Day, if anyone is doubting the competitiveness of City this season, just watch that game.

When it was 11 v 11, I thought United were the better team.

They pinned City back and were really bright going forward. Marcus Rashford, especially, was really positive and it felt like Michael Carrick's side were in the ascendancy.

The sending-off, which was the right decision by the way, kind of stopped United's momentum a little bit and also basically told City how they were going to have to play - they were going to have to defend for most of the game.

It is not what they are used to, but when you've got really experienced international players who are comfortable and calm, they don't really mind having to adapt.

They actually seemed to enjoy the challenge, and straight away they were well-organised and very disciplined.

United did not really create too much in the second part of the first half, other than a Rashford free-kick that hit the post, but I was thinking they would make a few tweaks at half-time and come out and really go after City. That didn't happen though.

United hit the post again in the second half, with Kobbie Mainoo's shot from distance, but they did not really create a clear-cut chance until Gianluigi Donnarumma saved from Bryan Mbeumo right at the end of the game.

Other than that, their decision-making in the final third wasn't great. They were shooting from silly angles or, when they got in some good wide areas and put the ball in, there were not enough numbers in the box.

United could also have changed their team around and brought on Benjamin Sesko earlier than they did, while I thought Rashford should have stayed on instead of Matheus Cunha because he was more of a threat.

But whatever United did try, City managed the game brilliantly.

Even at the time, I thought their winning goal really shouldn't have stood, because Enzo Fernandez impacts play and should have been ruled offside, but their defensive display was outstanding, and not just from their back four and central midfielders.

City were also superb further up the field. Antoine Semenyo and Erling Haaland were keeping the ball when it was played up to them, as well as winning free-kicks or beating people.

When he came on for Rayan Cherki, Iliman Ndiaye again did all of that brilliantly. He gave them a different dimension, and was a big reason they won the game.

That substitution was a clever one by Maresca and brave too, because while Ndiaye is better than Cherki defensively, he is also a ball-carrier who travels with the ball better too.

I remember Maresca making a couple of negative substitutions this time last year when his Chelsea side went down to 10 men early on at Old Trafford.

They ended up losing the game and he got a bit of criticism for it, but this time he went with Ndiaye, and it worked a treat.

He gave them an outlet and made some great runs - he was part of everything they did positively from an attacking point of view and was even involved in the goal - but also did his share of defending, and winning the ball back.

As the game went on, it looked like United were the ones who looked tired despite having the extra man for so long.

Maybe that was down to them playing on Thursday night, while City had their Champions League game on Tuesday, but it was not just energy that United were lacking.

They simply did not have the know-how to cause City problems. Let's not forget Donnarumma's late save because it was a brilliant stop, but Maresca's men were comfortable most of the time.

Danny Murphy was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

title: Zverev caps transformational year with US Open triumph
description: Alexander Zverev lands his second Grand Slam title after ending Ben Shelton's hopes of becoming a rare home US Open men's champion.
fullText:
Alexander Zverev used his greater experience to beat home hope Ben Shelton in the US Open final and quiet a partisan crowd hoping to laud a rare American men's champion.

German top seed Zverev lifted a heavy burden by winning his first major title at this year's French Open and has quickly added another with a 6-3 7-6 (7-2) 5-7 6-2 victory over Shelton in New York.

At the start of the season, there were question marks over whether 29-year-old Zverev would ever win one of the sport's most prestigious prizes.

Now he is celebrating becoming a multiple Grand Slam singles champion, having seen the path to glory partially cleared by injuries to Jannik Sinner and Carlos Alcaraz.

Sinner and Alcaraz swept the board between them at the majors in 2024 and 2025 - and Zverev has taken full advantage against the rest of the field in their absences.

Big-hitting Shelton, 23, has long been identified as a player who can win the biggest titles, but ultimately came up short in his first Grand Slam final against a rejuvenated Zverev.

Eighth seed Shelton was aiming to become the first American man to win a major singles title since Andy Roddick in 2003, but losing serve in the first game of the match set the tone as Zverev controlled the opening two sets.

The momentum shifted in the third set, however, as Shelton finally started applying serious pressure on Zverev's serve.

Taking his third break opportunity provided encouragement to the 24,000 home fans on Arthur Ashe Stadium, but starting the fourth set with a poor service game allowed Zverev to reassert his authority and extinguish American dreams.

Zverev did not initially know he had secured victory when Shelton hit a return long on championship point, only breaking out into a broad and slightly surprised smile after his team pointed out the score to him.

Zverev turns US Open tears into triumph

All About US Open: Zverev claims second Grand Slam title

Going into the 2026 season, few people would have backed Zverev to win two Grand Slam tournaments, with the German having already lost three major finals in a career which looked in danger of not living up to expectation.

But injuries to his biggest rivals - Alcaraz missing the French Open and Wimbledon, with Sinner ruled out of the US Open - opened the door for Zverev.

A below-par Zverev scraped through the opening rounds at Flushing Meadows in a series of early-morning finishes, but he gradually improved over a fortnight where he did not play a top-20 opponent until Shelton.

Zverev had not lost to Shelton in their five previous meetings and immediately capitalised on a nervy start by his opponent.

Shelton double-faulted on break point in the first game of the match, handing over the type of initiative that opponents often struggle to wrestle back from Zverev.

Through the strength of his first serve, and his ability to unpick Shelton's weaker backhand in the baseline exchanges, Zverev rolled through the opening set and clinched it when Shelton hit another double fault on set point.

Zverev continued to patiently draw mistakes from Shelton in the second set, but without being gifted a break when his only opportunity arrived in the fourth game.

He instead showed why he has a strong tie-break record with another nerveless display and, unlike in the 2020 US Open final when he lost from a two-set lead, kept his composure in the pressure moments to secure a commanding victory.

Addressing his team which is led by his father Alexander senior and brother Mischa, Zverev said: "We went 30 years without winning a Grand Slam title and now won two in the span of three months.

"I think God has seen how hard we have worked, how hard we have suffered and how much pain we went through.

"I think 2026 is the outcome of all the years that happened before."

Despite the bitter disappointment of losing Sunday's showpiece, Shelton will take pride from his run to a first major final, as well as further belief he can win a Grand Slam title.

Shelton came into the tournament with confidence after winning the Canadian Open last month, but also with a point to prove after an underwhelming season at the Grand Slams.

A chastening first-round exit at Wimbledon against Finnish qualifier Otto Virtanen was described by Shelton as "one of the toughest losses" of his career, acting as a wake-up call going into the North American hard court swing.

He has bounced back superbly to come close to ending America's 23-year wait for somebody to finally follow in Roddick's footsteps.

Shelton did not have an easy route to the final, needing to overcome a series of big-hitting opponents which included three former top-10 players as well as seven-time major champion Alcaraz.

Shelton had never beaten a top-three opponent until powering past Alcaraz - who was playing in his first tournament for almost five months - in an epic quarter-final which ended at 3:34am.

However, he could not double that tally against world number two Zverev.

Shelton's recent success has been a product of developing his defensive skills and improving his weaker backhand, but not being able to execute his damaging forehand in crucial moments against Zverev proved costly.

It was a reminder of the work the American number one still has to do at the highest level against the very best opponents.

"I'm excited with the progress that I feel that I've made, but this one stings 100%," said Shelton.

"I made too many errors when I had the ball there on my strings."
